lessons.title: Vector products, orientation and area
lessons.summary: Find a common normal, keep its orientation and use its magnitude geometrically.
lessons.objective: Calculate vector products and use them for normals, areas and coplanarity.
lessons.before: Review vector components, magnitudes and the scalar product. The determinant lesson supplies the alternating signs. Later lessons supply the line and plane methods used by some parts of the written practice.
lessons.ideas:
A perpendicular vector with an order

For non-parallel vectors u and v, their vector product is perpendicular to both. Its magnitude is \(|u||v|\sin\theta\); its direction follows the right-hand rule from u to v. Interchanging the factors reverses the result.

\[u\times v=\begin{pmatrix}u_2v_3-u_3v_2\\u_3v_1-u_1v_3\\u_1v_2-u_2v_1\end{pmatrix}.\]

Each dot product with a factor is zero: substituting the component formula makes the terms cancel in pairs. This checks perpendicularity but does not by itself check orientation. The zero vector has no direction and cannot be used as a normal.

Area comes from a perpendicular height

Choose two displacements sharing a vertex. Their parallelogram has area \(|u||v|\sin\theta\); a triangle has half that area.

\[A_{\triangle ABC}=\frac12\left|(b-a)\times(c-a)\right|.\]

Parallel sides give zero area. A unit normal is either sign of \((u\times v)/|u\times v|\); retain the sign or component restriction in the question.

Coplanarity and a geometric extension

Three non-collinear points A,B,C determine a plane. A fourth point D belongs to it exactly when its displacement from A has no component along the normal:

\[(d-a)\cdot\big((b-a)\times(c-a)\big)=0.\]

First check the normal is non-zero; collinear A,B,C do not determine a unique plane. For a tetrahedron, base area times perpendicular height divided by three gives the derived extension

\[V=\frac16\left|(d-a)\cdot\big((b-a)\times(c-a)\big)\right|.\]

This follows from the base-and-height argument; a separately memorised named product is unnecessary.

Solving a vector-product equation

If \(w\times u=b\) with \(u\ne0\), necessarily \(b\cdot u=0\). Write the three component equations to find one solution. Adding any multiple of u leaves the product unchanged. Conversely, subtracting two solutions gives a vector parallel to u. An extra scalar-product condition may select one member of this family.
lessons.method:
1. Form displacement vectors, keeping their order.
  2. Calculate the three components and check both scalar products.
  3. Check non-degeneracy and the required orientation.
  4. Use the magnitude for area, or project a displacement onto the normal.
mistakes: Reversing the factors changes the sign.
A normal may be rescaled, but a requested vector product may not.
Use displacements from a shared vertex for a triangle.
A zero normal does not define a plane.

examples.title: 1 · Check both perpendicularity and orientation
examples.question: Find \(u\times v\) for \(u=(2,1,-1)^T\), \(v=(1,-2,3)^T\), and a unit vector in that direction.
examples.solution:
\[u\times v=(1,-7,-5)^T.\]

The dot products are \(2-7+5=0\) and \(1+14-15=0\). The magnitude is \(\sqrt{75}=5\sqrt3\), so the required unit vector is

\[\frac1{5\sqrt3}(1,-7,-5)^T.\]

The negative is also perpendicular, but has the opposite orientation.

examples.title: 2 · Area and an altitude from one calculation
examples.question: Find the area of triangle \(ABC\), where \(A=(1,0,2)\), \(B=(3,1,2)\), \(C=(2,-1,4)\), and the perpendicular distance from C to AB.
examples.solution:
Use \(AB=(2,1,0)^T\) and \(AC=(1,-1,2)^T\). Their product is \((2,-4,-3)^T\), of magnitude \(\sqrt{29}\). Thus

\[A=\frac{\sqrt{29}}2,\qquad h=\frac{\sqrt{29}}{\sqrt5}=\frac{\sqrt{145}}5.\]

The height uses AB as its base; changing the base would change the altitude.

examples.title: 3 · Retain the non-collinearity check
examples.question: For \(A=(0,1,0)\), \(B=(1,1,1)\), \(C=(0,2,1)\) and \(D=(k,0,2)\), find k for coplanarity.
examples.solution:
\[AB\times AC=(-1,-1,1)^T\ne0.\]

Hence ABC determines a plane. The condition on \(AD=(k,-1,2)^T\) is \(-k+1+2=0\), giving \(k=3\). The test works because the first three points are non-collinear.

examples.title: 4 · Derive a volume from area and height
examples.question: Find the volume of \(OABC\), with \(A=(2,0,0)\), \(B=(0,3,0)\), \(C=(1,1,4)\).
examples.solution: OAB has area 3 and lies in \(z=0\). C has perpendicular height 4, so \(V=\frac13(3)(4)=4\). Equivalently, \(OA\times OB=(0,0,6)^T\); its scalar product with OC is 24, and \(24/6=4\). The absolute value makes a volume positive.

lessons.title: Lines and common perpendiculars
lessons.summary: Use independent parameters to distinguish intersection, parallelism and skewness.
lessons.objective: Find perpendicular feet and the shortest distance between lines, treating parallel lines separately.
lessons.before: Review vector products, scalar products and simultaneous linear equations. Some written problems also use the following plane lessons; return to their plane parts after studying those methods.
lessons.ideas:
A point and a non-zero direction

A line has equation \(r=a+s\,u\), with \(u\ne0\) and real s. Two given points give a direction by subtraction. Changing the anchor along the line, or rescaling its direction with a corresponding change of parameter, describes the same locus.

Classify before applying a distance formula

For \(r=a+s\,u\) and \(r=b+t\,v\), use separate parameters. If \(u\times v=0\), the lines are parallel; they coincide exactly when \((b-a)\times u=0\). For non-parallel directions, zero \((b-a)\cdot(u\times v)\) means the two lines are coplanar and intersect. Otherwise they are skew.

The nearest point on a line

The foot \(H=a+s\,u\) from P satisfies \((p-H)\cdot u=0\), giving

\[s=\frac{(p-a)\cdot u}{u\cdot u},\qquad d=|p-H|.\]

Equivalently, triangle area gives \(d=|(p-a)\times u|/|u|\). The line is infinite: do not impose a segment restriction unless requested.

Two perpendicular feet

Write \(P=a+s\,u\), \(Q=b+t\,v\). The shortest connector is perpendicular to each line, so solve

\[(Q-P)\cdot u=0,\qquad (Q-P)\cdot v=0.\]

The coefficient determinant is non-zero for non-parallel directions, giving a unique pair of feet. A common perpendicular then passes through P in direction Q−P. Its direction is parallel to \(u\times v\).

Distance as a normal projection

\[d=\frac{|(b-a)\cdot(u\times v)|}{|u\times v|}\quad(u\times v\ne0).\]

Every connector has the same normal component because changing s or t adds a line direction, perpendicular to the normal. The perpendicular connector attains that lower bound. For parallel lines the displayed formula is undefined; use a point-to-line distance instead. Distinct parallel lines have infinitely many shortest joining segments.
lessons.method:
1. Identify both anchors and both non-zero directions.
  2. Test parallelism and intersection before choosing a formula.
  3. For feet, solve both perpendicularity equations.
  4. Check membership on the original lines and the connector length.
mistakes: Different lines need independent parameters.
A zero numerator means intersection only when the cross product is non-zero.
The skew-line formula cannot be used for parallel directions.
A shortest distance alone does not give the two feet.

examples.title: 1 · Recover a parameter from all coordinates
examples.question: Give a line through \(A=(2,-1,3)\), \(B=(5,1,2)\), and decide whether \(P=(8,3,1)\) lies on it.
examples.solution:
\[r=(2,-1,3)^T+s(3,2,-1)^T.\]

The x-coordinate of P gives \(s=2\). The same value gives y=3 and z=1, so P belongs to the line. Checking only one coordinate would be insufficient.

examples.title: 2 · Find the full perpendicular foot
examples.question: Find the foot from \(P=(4,1,5)\) to \(r=(1,-1,2)^T+s(1,2,2)^T\), and its distance.
examples.solution:
The perpendicularity equation is \(13-9s=0\), so \(s=13/9\). Therefore

\[H=(22/9,17/9,44/9),\qquad d=\frac{\sqrt{29}}3.\]

The displacement \(P-H=(14,-8,1)^T/9\) has zero dot product with \((1,2,2)^T\). This checks both the point and the distance.

examples.title: 3 · Locate both ends of a skew separation
examples.question: Find the shortest joining segment between \(r=(1,0,0)^T+s(1,1,0)^T\) and \(r=(0,2,3)^T+t(1,-1,0)^T\).
examples.solution:
The perpendicularity equations give \(s=1/2\), \(t=3/2\). Thus

\[P=(3/2,1/2,0),\qquad Q=(3/2,1/2,3).\]

The connector is \((0,0,3)^T\), perpendicular to both directions, and its length is 3. Their direction product is \((0,0,-2)^T\), and the non-zero normal separation confirms the lines are skew.

examples.title: 4 · Parallel lines have a family of feet
examples.question: Find the distance between \(r=(0,1,0)^T+s(1,0,1)^T\) and \(r=(1,3,0)^T+t(2,0,2)^T\). Describe every closest pair.
examples.solution:
The directions are parallel. The foot of the second anchor B on the first line is \(H=(1/2,1,1/2)\). Hence \(d=3\sqrt2/2\). Every closest pair has the form

\[P=H+\lambda(1,0,1)^T,\]\[Q=B+\lambda(1,0,1)^T.\]

The connector remains \((1/2,2,-1/2)^T\), perpendicular to the common direction. Conversely, perpendicularity forces equal displacement along that direction.

lessons.title: Describing and intersecting planes
lessons.summary: Turn independent directions into a normal, and check every defining condition.
lessons.objective: Convert plane descriptions and find complete line–plane and plane–plane intersections.
lessons.before: Review common normals and line equations. A plane requires two independent directions, not merely two listed vectors.
lessons.ideas:
Equivalent descriptions of one plane

Through a point a with non-zero normal n, all plane points satisfy \((r-a)\cdot n=0\). Thus \(n\cdot r=d\), where \(d=n\cdot a\). In components, \(Ax+By+Cz=D\), with \((A,B,C)\ne(0,0,0)\). Multiplying all four coefficients by one non-zero scalar leaves the plane unchanged.

A two-parameter description is \(r=a+s\,u+t\,v\), with \(u\times v\ne0\). Its normal is \(u\times v\). For points A,B,C, use \(u=b-a\) and \(v=c-a\). Parallel directions would describe a line instead.

Substituting a line

For \(r=a+s\,u\) and \(n\cdot r=d\), substitution gives

\[s(n\cdot u)=d-n\cdot a.\]

A non-zero coefficient gives one intersection. If it is zero, check the remaining constant: zero gives containment, non-zero gives parallel disjointness. Do not divide before making this distinction.

Intersecting two planes

For independent normals \(n_1,n_2\), the intersection direction is \(n_1\times n_2\). Find one point satisfying both equations, then combine it with that direction. Setting a convenient coordinate to zero is allowed only if the resulting equations are consistent; otherwise choose another free coordinate.

Verify the anchor satisfies both planes and the direction is perpendicular to both normals. Parallel normals require a separate check for coincident or disjoint planes; they do not give an intersection line.

A plane containing an entire line

Check both its anchor and its direction: \(n\cdot a=d\) and \(n\cdot u=0\). A plane perpendicular to a line has normal parallel to that line's direction. A plane perpendicular to another plane has a normal perpendicular to the other normal. Combine the required conditions before choosing a normal.
lessons.method:
1. List the required points and directions.
  2. Find a non-zero normal or two independent plane directions.
  3. Use a defining point to find the plane constant.
  4. For intersections, solve and substitute into every original equation.
mistakes: A plane normal is not generally a direction in the plane.
Two parallel vectors do not determine a plane.
Rescale the constant together with the normal coefficients.
A failed convenient coordinate choice does not imply disjoint planes.

examples.title: 1 · Build a plane through three points
examples.question: Find a plane through \(A=(1,0,2)\), \(B=(2,1,2)\), \(C=(1,1,3)\).
examples.solution:
The directions \((1,1,0)^T\), \((0,1,1)^T\) have product \((1,-1,1)^T\). Dotting it with A gives 3. Hence

\[x-y+z=3.\]

Both other points satisfy the equation, and the non-zero normal confirms uniqueness.

examples.title: 2 · Convert a two-parameter description
examples.question: Convert \(r=(0,2,1)^T+s(1,1,0)^T+t(0,1,2)^T\) to scalar-product and Cartesian form.
examples.solution:
The normal is \((2,-2,1)^T\); its scalar product with the anchor is −3. Thus

\[r\cdot(2,-2,1)^T=-3,\]\[2x-2y+z=-3.\]

The two directions are independent. Dividing all coefficients, including −3, by one non-zero number gives an equivalent equation.

examples.title: 3 · Verify an entire intersection line
examples.question: Find the intersection of \(x+y+z=4\) and \(x-y+z=2\).
examples.solution:
Subtracting gives y=1, then x+z=3. Choose x=0 for the anchor and let x vary as s:

\[r=(0,1,3)^T+s(1,0,-1)^T.\]

The anchor satisfies both equations. The direction has zero scalar product with both normals. These two checks verify every point of the line, not just the anchor.

examples.title: 4 · Find the unique crossing point
examples.question: Intersect \(r=(2,0,1)^T+t(1,2,-1)^T\) with \(x-y+z=5\).
examples.solution: Substitution gives \(3-2t=5\), so t=−1. The point is \(X=(1,-2,2)\), and \(1-(-2)+2=5\). The coefficient −2 is non-zero, so this is the only intersection.

lessons.title: Angles, projections and distances
lessons.summary: Choose a normal component or a tangential component to match the geometry.
lessons.objective: Find angles, perpendicular feet, projections and reflections with correct signs and complete coordinates.
lessons.before: Review plane equations and perpendicular feet on lines. Angles between a line and a plane differ from angles between their direction and normal.
lessons.ideas:
Angles use the right pair of directions

For the smaller angle between two lines, use the absolute scalar product of their directions. For planes, use their normals:

\[\cos\beta=\frac{|n_1\cdot n_2|}{|n_1||n_2|}.\]

For a line direction u and plane normal n, the line–plane angle is complementary to the direction–normal angle:

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|u\cdot n|}{|u||n|},\quad0\le\alpha\le\pi/2.\]

Check non-zero directions and normals. Parallel and perpendicular configurations attain the endpoints, rather than an acute interior angle.

Distance and foot on a plane

For \(n\cdot r=d\), removing the normal component of p gives

\[H=p-\frac{n\cdot p-d}{n\cdot n}\,n,\] \[\operatorname{dist}(P,\Pi)=\frac{|n\cdot p-d|}{|n|}.\]

The residual itself is signed; distance needs its absolute value. Verify H lies in the plane and P−H is parallel to its normal. Reflection is \(R=2H-P\).

Projecting or reflecting an entire line

Apply the point map to \(a+t\,u\) and collect the constant and t terms. Projection sends the direction to \(u-(n\cdot u)n/(n\cdot n)\); reflection subtracts twice that normal component. A zero projected direction means the projected locus is one point, not a line. A reflected direction cannot vanish when u is non-zero.

Equal distances and minimum routes

The locus equidistant from two distinct points is their perpendicular bisector plane; expanding the squared distances cancels the quadratic terms. Equal distances to two planes give two signed equations after dividing each residual by its normal's magnitude. For a route touching a plane, reflection and the triangle inequality can establish a global minimum, but equality must occur on the required segment.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the required angle or distance.
  2. Use a non-zero normal and the appropriate scalar product.
  3. Recover all requested coordinates, not only a length.
  4. Check membership, perpendicularity, signs and any equality conditions.
mistakes: Line–plane angles use sine; plane–plane angles use cosine.
Distance is non-negative even when a residual is negative.
Reflection moves twice the distance to the perpendicular foot.
A projected line can collapse to one point.

examples.title: 1 · Distance, foot and reflection together
examples.question: For \(P=(5,1,2)\) and \(\Pi:2x-y+2z=4\), find the perpendicular foot, distance and reflection.
examples.solution:
The normal is \(n=(2,-1,2)^T\), with \(n\cdot n=9\) and residual 9. Therefore

\[H=P-n=(3,2,0),\qquad d=3,\]\[R=2H-P=(1,3,-2).\]

The midpoint of P,R is H; both displacements are normal to the plane.

examples.title: 2 · Distinguish the two angle formulae
examples.question: A line has direction \((1,2,2)^T\). Find its smaller angle with a plane of normal \((2,-1,2)^T\). Also find the smaller angle between this plane and one of normal \((1,1,0)^T\), to 1 decimal place.
examples.solution:
For the line–plane angle, \(\sin\alpha=4/9\), giving \(\alpha=26.4^\circ\). For the plane–plane angle,

\[\cos\beta=\frac1{3\sqrt2},\qquad\beta=76.4^\circ.\]

The different trigonometric functions reflect different geometric angles.

examples.title: 3 · Project a whole line without losing its parameter
examples.question: Project \(r=(5,1,2)^T+t(1,2,2)^T\) orthogonally onto \(2x-y+2z=4\).
examples.solution:
The projected anchor is \((3,2,0)^T\). Remove the normal component of the direction:

\[u_{\parallel}=(1,2,2)^T-\frac49(2,-1,2)^T=\frac19(1,22,10)^T.\]

Thus the projection is

\[r=(3,2,0)^T+\frac t9(1,22,10)^T.\]

The direction is non-zero and perpendicular to the plane normal. Replacing t/9 by a new real parameter gives the same line, but changes the correspondence of parameters.

examples.title: 4 · Recover a plane from equal distances
examples.question: Find the locus of points equidistant from \(A=(1,0,0)\), \(B=(3,2,0)\). Then find both angle-bisector planes of \(x+y=3\) and \(x-y=1\).
examples.solution:
The first locus has normal \(B-A=(2,2,0)^T\) and contains the midpoint \((2,1,0)\), so it is \(x+y=3\). The two given plane normals have equal magnitude. Hence their equal-distance condition is

\[|x+y-3|=|x-y-1|.\]

Taking the two signs gives \(y=1\) or \(x=2\), with no restriction on z. Keeping only one sign would omit half the locus.

lessons.title: Parameters and exceptional configurations
lessons.summary: Classify the geometry before cancelling a factor or taking a limit.
lessons.objective: Find all admissible parameter values and describe exceptional lines, planes and loci completely.
lessons.before: Review line classification, plane intersections and distance formulae. Every parameter value must still define the objects in the question.
lessons.ideas:
Check whether the object exists

A line needs a non-zero direction. A Cartesian plane needs a non-zero normal. Two directions give a plane only if their vector product is non-zero. Record the values where these conditions fail before applying a formula.

Separate the exceptional equations

In a line–plane substitution \(A(k)t=B(k)\), first solve \(A(k)=0\). At each such value, \(B(k)=0\) gives containment; otherwise there is no intersection. For the other values solve \(t=B(k)/A(k)\). A cancelled factor can hide a whole contained line.

Distance conditions need both signs

A positive target distance can lie on either side of a plane. Squaring an absolute-value equation is legitimate when its denominator is defined and both sides are non-negative; check the original equation and all restrictions afterwards. If two directions become parallel, recompute their distance with a point-to-line method.

State the whole locus, including omissions

A parametrised result may resemble a complete line but omit points. Determine the range of the new parameter and prove a converse: every retained point should come from an allowed original parameter. A limiting point need not be attained. Different geometry at an exceptional value can make a distance discontinuous there.

Completeness is part of the answer

Give every valid root, both signed distance cases and every permitted branch of a trigonometric parameter interval. Explain whether exceptional planes coincide, intersect or are parallel; do not label all zero determinants as the same configuration.
lessons.method:
1. Find values making a direction, normal or denominator vanish.
  2. Classify those configurations directly.
  3. Solve the non-degenerate equation with all signs and domain restrictions.
  4. Check every candidate in the original geometry and describe any omitted locus points.
mistakes: Do not substitute into a formula that became undefined.
A zero intersection coefficient can mean containment or disjointness.
Squaring does not remove the need to check restrictions.
An unattained limiting point is not part of a locus.

examples.title: 1 · A contained line, a parallel line and two missing points
examples.question: Classify \(r=(k,0,0)^T+t(k(k-2),1,0)^T\) relative to \(x=0\). Describe the locus of unique intersection points.
examples.solution: Substitution gives \(k+k(k-2)t=0\). At k=0 the line is contained; at k=2 it is parallel and disjoint. Otherwise \(t=-1/(k-2)\), giving \(X=(0,-1/(k-2),0)\). Its y-coordinate takes every real value except 0 and 1/2: zero is unattainable, while 1/2 would require k=0. Conversely \(k=2-1/y\) recovers every retained point.

examples.title: 2 · Retain both sides of a plane
examples.question: Find all k for which \(P=(k,1,2)\) has distance 2 from \(x+2y-2z=0\).
examples.solution:
\[\frac{|k-2|}{3}=2.\]

Thus \(k-2=\pm6\), giving \(k=-4\) or \(k=8\). Both satisfy the original distance condition. Giving one value would select only one side of the plane.

examples.title: 3 · Recompute the distance at a parallel value
examples.question: Find the distance between \(r=s(1,0,0)^T\) and \(r=(0,2,1)^T+t(1,k,0)^T\) for every real k.
examples.solution: If \(k\ne0\), the common normal is \((0,0,k)^T\), giving distance 1. At k=0 the directions are parallel, and the nearest connector is \((0,2,1)^T\), of length \(\sqrt5\). The distance is therefore 1 for \(k\ne0\), and \(\sqrt5\) for k=0. The non-parallel formula divides by zero at k=0; its limiting value does not answer that case.

examples.title: 4 · Coincident planes are not an intersection line
examples.question: Classify the intersection of \(x+y+z=2\) and \((k-1)x+y+z=2\) for every real k.
examples.solution: Subtracting gives \((k-2)x=0\). When \(k\ne2\), the intersection is the line \(x=0,\ y+z=2\), for example \(r=(0,2,0)^T+t(0,-1,1)^T\). When k=2 the equations coincide, so the intersection is the whole plane. Neither normal vanishes, but the normals become parallel; division by k−2 would lose that case.

questions.title: Give the oriented vector product
questions.prompt_html: Find \(u\times v\), for \(u=\left[\begin{matrix}3\\1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(v=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\). Enter all three components in this order.
questions.answer_html: Product component x: \(2\); Product component y: \(-6\); Product component z: \(-4\)
questions.solution_html:
\[u\times v=\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-6\\-4\end{matrix}\right].\]

Both dot products vanish; reversing the order would give the negative.
questions.hint_html: Identify the points and non-zero directions first. Give every requested coordinate or parameter value, and check the original geometric conditions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the complete correct product component x.
Give the complete correct product component y.
Give the complete correct product component z.

questions.title: Area and the corresponding altitude
questions.prompt_html: For \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\), \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}4\\2\\0\end{matrix}\right]\), \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}2\\0\\2\end{matrix}\right]\), find the area of ABC and the perpendicular distance from C to AB.
questions.answer_html: Triangle area: \(\sqrt{14}\); Distance from C to AB: \(\frac{2 \sqrt{35}}{5}\)
questions.solution_html: The magnitude of \(AB\times AC\) is \(2 \sqrt{14}\). Halve it for area and divide it by \(|AB|=\sqrt{10}\) for height.
questions.hint_html: Identify the points and non-zero directions first. Give every requested coordinate or parameter value, and check the original geometric conditions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the complete correct distance from c to ab.

questions.title: Coplanarity before volume
questions.prompt_html: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]\), \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\0\end{matrix}\right]\), \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\\2\end{matrix}\right]\), \(D=(k,1,1)^T\). Find k for coplanarity. Then find the tetrahedron volume when \(k=3\).
questions.answer_html: Coplanar k-value: \(1\); Volume when k=3: \(\frac{4}{3}\)
questions.solution_html: ABC is the plane x=1, so coplanarity requires k=1. Its triangular area is 2. For the volume part the perpendicular height is 2, giving \(\frac{4}{3}\).
questions.hint_html: Identify the points and non-zero directions first. Give every requested coordinate or parameter value, and check the original geometric conditions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the complete correct volume when k=3.

questions.title: Check orientation and non-degeneracy
questions.prompt_html: For non-parallel u,v, which statement is correct?
questions.answer_html: Correct statement: B
questions.solution_html: Order fixes the orientation. A zero cross product means dependent directions and cannot define a plane normal.
questions.hint_html: Identify the points and non-zero directions first. Give every requested coordinate or parameter value, and check the original geometric conditions.

options.A: v × u has the same direction as u × v.
options.B: v × u is the negative of u × v.
options.C: Every vector perpendicular to u is equal to u × v.

questions.title: Find the whole perpendicular foot
questions.prompt_html: Find the foot H from \(P=\left[\begin{matrix}5\\3\\3\end{matrix}\right]\) to \(r=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\\1\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\), and the exact distance PH.
questions.answer_html: Foot coordinate x: \(3\); Foot coordinate y: \(4\); Foot coordinate z: \(3\); Perpendicular distance: \(\sqrt{5}\)
questions.solution_html: The zero scalar-product condition gives t=2. Thus \(H=\left[\begin{matrix}3\\4\\3\end{matrix}\right]\), and \(PH=\sqrt{5}\).
questions.hint_html: Identify the points and non-zero directions first. Give every requested coordinate or parameter value, and check the original geometric conditions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the complete correct foot coordinate x.
Give the complete correct foot coordinate y.
Give the complete correct foot coordinate z.

questions.title: Calculate the skew separation
questions.prompt_html: Find the exact shortest distance between \(r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(r=\left[\begin{matrix}-1\\8\\3\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\\-1\end{matrix}\right]\).
questions.answer_html: Exact shortest distance: \(2 \sqrt{3}\)
questions.solution_html: The directions have product \(\left[\begin{matrix}-2\\2\\-2\end{matrix}\right]\ne0\). The normal projection gives \(d=2 \sqrt{3}\); its non-zero value confirms skewness.
questions.hint_html: Identify the points and non-zero directions first. Give every requested coordinate or parameter value, and check the original geometric conditions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the complete correct exact shortest distance.

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-4\\5\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-6\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}t - 7\\t - 5\\9\end{pmatrix}\]

The parameter \(t\) is real.

  1. Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\).

    [2]

  2. Find the value of \(t\) for which \(A,B,C,D\) are coplanar.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}10\\10\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[t=3\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Subtract the position vector of A from those of B and C, then calculate

\[\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}10\\10\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

The non-zero vector product gives a normal to plane ABC. Thus D is in this plane exactly when

\[\overrightarrow{AD}\cdot\mathbf n=0\]
\[2 \left(t - 3\right)=0\]

The non-zero normal also confirms that A, B and C are not collinear.

(b)

questions.title: Locate the common perpendicular
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-6\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-3\\1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

  1. The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors.

    [6]

  2. Hence give a vector equation of the common perpendicular.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- 2 \lambda + \mu + 6\\- 3 \lambda + \mu + 3\\3 - 2 \lambda\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 17 \lambda + 5 \mu + 27=0\]
\[- 5 \lambda + 2 \mu + 9=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=1,\qquad\mu=-2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

(b)

The joining direction is \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), perpendicular to both line directions. Using the foot \(\left(2,-3,0\right)\) gives

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

Substitution of the second foot confirms that it lies on the same line.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use two independent parameters and require the joining vector to have zero dot product with both directions.

(b)

Use either foot as the anchor, and the vector product of the line directions as the direction.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use a correct foot as an anchor.
Give a full equation with the common-normal direction.

questions.title: Shortest distance and its two endpoints
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}6\\0\\13\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

  1. Show that \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are skew, and find their exact shortest distance.

    [3]

  2. The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors.

    [6]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[d=2 \sqrt{29}\]

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\4\\11\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

A common perpendicular direction is

\[\mathbf n=\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]

Project the connector between the two given anchors onto this normal:

\[d=\frac{|(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|-58|}{\sqrt{29}}=2 \sqrt{29}\]

The vector product is non-zero and the scalar product is non-zero, so the lines are non-parallel and non-coplanar: they are skew.

(b)

Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- 3 \lambda + \mu + 12\\2 \left(\lambda - \mu - 1\right)\\\mu + 10\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 13 \lambda + 7 \mu + 40=0\]
\[- 7 \lambda + 6 \mu + 26=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=2,\qquad\mu=-2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\4\\11\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\6\\8\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Find a vector perpendicular to both directions, and project a joining vector onto it.

(b)

Use two independent parameters and require the joining vector to have zero dot product with both directions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Project the anchor connector onto the unit normal. Obtain \(2 \sqrt{29}\) and justify that the lines are skew.

questions.title: A moving line and an exact distance condition
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-4\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}2 - t\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

Here \(t\) is real. Let \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=CD\).

  1. Find the shortest distance between \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) as a function of \(t\).

    [3]

  2. Find all real values of \(t\) for which the shortest distance is \(\frac{7 \sqrt{11}}{11}\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[d(t)=\frac{|- t - 3|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 2 t + 3}}\]

(b)

\[t=\frac{6}{19}\quad\text{or}\quad4\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The line directions have vector product

\[\mathbf n(t)=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1 - t\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

This vector never vanishes. The anchor connector has scalar product \(- t - 3\) with it, so the perpendicular separation is

\[d(t)=\frac{|- t - 3|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 2 t + 3}}\]

A zero numerator corresponds to intersecting, not skew, lines; the same expression then gives distance zero.

(b)

Use the distance expression obtained above.

\[\frac{|- t - 3|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 2 t + 3}}=\frac{7 \sqrt{11}}{11}\]

Both sides are non-negative and the denominator is strictly positive, so squaring introduces no additional sign condition:

\[- \frac{2 \left(t - 4\right) \left(19 t - 6\right)}{11}=0\]

Solving gives

\[t=\frac{6}{19}\quad\text{or}\quad4\]

Substitution of each value in the original distance formula gives \(\frac{7 \sqrt{11}}{11}\). Both values are admissible.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the vector product of the directions and project the anchor connector onto it.

(b)

Keep the absolute value until squaring, and check every candidate in the original distance condition.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the absolute normal component of the connector. Obtain \(|- t - 3|/\sqrt{t^{2} - 2 t + 3}\).
Obtain the factorised equation \(- \frac{2 \left(t - 4\right) \left(19 t - 6\right)}{11}=0\). Find and check all roots \(\frac{6}{19},4\).

questions.title: A family with contained, parallel and crossing cases
questions.prompt_html:
For each real \(t\), a line \(l_t\) has equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}t\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}t^{2} - 5 t + 7\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

The fixed plane \(\Pi\) has equation

\[x + 3 y - z=-2\]

For parts (b) and (c), take \(t=6\).

  1. Classify the position of \(l_t\) relative to \(\Pi\) for every real \(t\).

    [5]

  2. Find \(X\), the point where \(l_t\) meets \(\Pi\).

    [2]

  3. Find the acute angle between \(l_t\) and \(\Pi\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(t=1\): the entire line lies in \(\Pi\). \(t=4\): parallel and disjoint. All other real values: a unique intersection.

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{1}{2}\\\frac{1}{2}\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{1870}}{187}\right)=13.4^\circ\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Substitution into the plane equation gives

\[\left(t - 1\right) \left(\lambda t - 4 \lambda + 1\right)=0\]

If \(t=1\), this is true for every \(\lambda\), so the line is contained. If \(t=4\), the left side is the non-zero constant \(3\), so there is no intersection. Otherwise it gives exactly one value of \(\lambda\).

(b)

Substitute the line into the plane equation:

\[3+(10)\lambda=-2\]
\[\lambda=- \frac{1}{2}\]

Since \(10\)\(\ne0\), there is exactly one intersection. Substitution into the line gives

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{1}{2}\\\frac{1}{2}\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Use the line direction and plane normal:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}13\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

The angle between a line and a plane is the complement of the angle between its direction and the plane normal. Therefore use sine, not cosine.

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|10|}{\sqrt{1870}}=\frac{\sqrt{1870}}{187}\]
\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{1870}}{187}\right)=13.4^\circ\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Do not cancel a parameter factor until its zero case has been considered.

(b)

Insert the line coordinates into the plane equation, solve for the parameter, then substitute back.

(c)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

marking_criteria.description_html: Substitute the line into the plane equation.
Substitute the line into the plane equation.

questions.title: A moving line and an exact distance condition
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\3\\5\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\t + 4\\6\end{pmatrix}\]

Here \(t\) is real. Let \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=CD\).

For part (b) only, use \(t=0\).

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of \(ABC\).

    [4]

  2. Find the acute angle between \(ABC\) and \(ABD\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]

  3. Find the shortest distance between \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) as a function of \(t\).

    [5]

  4. Find all real values of \(t\) for which the shortest distance is \(\sqrt{2}\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[x + y + 2 z=11\]

(b)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}\right)=19.5^\circ\]

(c)

\[d(t)=\frac{|- t - 2|}{\sqrt{t^{2} + 2}}\]

(d)

\[t=0\quad\text{or}\quad4\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}=11\]

Using the point \(\left(0,3,4\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[x + y + 2 z=11\]

(b)

For plane \(ABD\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|4|}{3 \sqrt{2}}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}\right)=19.5^\circ\]

(c)

The line directions have vector product

\[\mathbf n(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\- t\end{pmatrix}\]

This vector never vanishes. The anchor connector has scalar product \(- t - 2\) with it, so the perpendicular separation is

\[d(t)=\frac{|- t - 2|}{\sqrt{t^{2} + 2}}\]

A zero numerator corresponds to intersecting, not skew, lines; the same expression then gives distance zero.

(d)

Use the distance expression obtained above.

\[\frac{|- t - 2|}{\sqrt{t^{2} + 2}}=\sqrt{2}\]

Both sides are non-negative and the denominator is strictly positive, so squaring introduces no additional sign condition:

\[- t \left(t - 4\right)=0\]

Solving gives

\[t=0\quad\text{or}\quad4\]

Substitution of each value in the original distance formula gives \(\sqrt{2}\). Both values are admissible.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(b)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

(c)

Use the vector product of the directions and project the anchor connector onto it.

(d)

Keep the absolute value until squaring, and check every candidate in the original distance condition.

questions.title: Reflecting a point and an entire line
questions.prompt_html:
The plane \(\Pi\) has equation \(6 x + 5 y + 2 z=-9\). Point \(P\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}8\\11\\9\end{pmatrix}\), and \(l\) is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}8\\11\\9\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}7\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

  1. Find the position vector of \(H\), the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) to the plane. Hence find the reflection \(R\) of \(P\) in the plane.

    [5]

  2. Find a vector equation of the reflection of \(l\) in the plane, explaining how its direction is obtained.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\1\\5\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OR}=\begin{pmatrix}-16\\-9\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-16\\-9\\1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-7\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\5\\2\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

\[121-65\tau=-9\]
\[\tau=2\]

Therefore

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\1\\5\end{pmatrix}\]

The foot is the midpoint of the original point and its reflection:

\[\mathbf r=2\mathbf h-\mathbf p=\begin{pmatrix}-16\\-9\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

For any point \(\mathbf x\), its reflection in the plane is

\[\mathbf x^*=\mathbf x-2\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf x-d}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n\]

Insert \(\mathbf x=\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w\) and collect the constant and parameter terms:

\[\mathbf p^*=\begin{pmatrix}-16\\-9\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf w^*=\mathbf w-2\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf w}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-7\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence the image line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-16\\-9\\1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-7\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The perpendicular direction is the plane normal. A reflection uses the foot as the midpoint.

(b)

Reflect a general point on the line, not only the anchor.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use a line through \(P\) in the normal direction.
Substitute this line into the plane equation.
Use the midpoint relationship \(\mathbf r=2\mathbf h-\mathbf p\). Obtain the reflected point \(\left(-16,-9,1\right)\).
Reflect the anchor using its perpendicular foot.
Reflect the direction, reversing its normal component.

questions.title: A family through an intersection line
questions.prompt_html:
The planes \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\) have equations

\[x - z=0\]
\[2 \left(x + y\right)=20\]

The family \(\Pi_k\) is defined by

\[2 k x + 2 k y + x - z=20 k\]

Plane \(\Sigma\) has normal \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\0\end{pmatrix}\). Point \(P\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\3\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).

    [4]

  2. Find the member of the family perpendicular to \(\Sigma\), explaining why it contains the line from (a).

    [3]

  3. Find the exact perpendicular distance from \(P\) to \(\Pi_{- \frac{1}{5}}\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\10\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[k=- \frac{1}{5}\]
\[\frac{3 x - 2 y - 5 z}{5}=-4\]

(c)

\[d=\frac{9 \sqrt{38}}{19}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

A direction of the intersection is perpendicular to both normals:

\[\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence we may take direction \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Solving the two plane equations with a convenient coordinate set to zero gives the point \(\left(0,10,0\right)\). It satisfies both equations:

\[0=0,\qquad 20=20\]

The required line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\10\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Every member contains the line found in (a), since its equation is the sum of the two original equations after multiplying the second by \(k\). Perpendicular planes have perpendicular normals:

\[2 \left(5 k + 1\right)=0\]
\[k=- \frac{1}{5}\]
\[\frac{3 x - 2 y - 5 z}{5}=-4\]

(c)

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{3}{5}\\- \frac{2}{5}\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|\frac{18}{5}|}{\frac{\sqrt{38}}{5}}=\frac{9 \sqrt{38}}{19}\]

The absolute value ensures a non-negative distance.

(b)

Use a zero dot product of the two plane normals.

(c)

Divide the absolute residual in the plane equation by the length of its normal.

questions.title: A plane normal, a foot and an inclination

The parameters \(s\) and \(t\) are real.

The point \(P\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-8\\4\end{pmatrix}\). The line \(l\) is parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi\).

    [4]

  2. Find the position vector of \(H\), the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) to the plane.

    [4]

  3. Find the acute angle between \(l\) and \(\Pi\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]

(a)

\[x - 2 y - z=8\]

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-6\\5\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{66}}{11}\right)=47.6^\circ\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\6\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\-1\end{pmatrix}=8\]

Using the point \(\left(1,-3,-1\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[x - 2 y - z=8\]

(b)

The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

\[14-6\tau=8\]
\[\tau=1\]

Therefore

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-6\\5\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Use the line direction and plane normal:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

The angle between a line and a plane is the complement of the angle between its direction and the plane normal. Therefore use sine, not cosine.

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|6|}{\sqrt{66}}=\frac{\sqrt{66}}{11}\]
\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{66}}{11}\right)=47.6^\circ\]

questions.title: A bisector plane between skew lines
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\9\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\6\\2\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

The common perpendicular meets the lines at \(P\) and \(Q\). Let \(\Pi\) be the perpendicular bisector plane of \(PQ\).

  1. The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors.

    [6]

  2. Find the equation of \(\Pi\) and explain why its points are equidistant from \(P\) and \(Q\).

    [4]

  3. Find the two planes parallel to \(\Pi\) that contain \(l_1\) and \(l_2\), respectively. Find their perpendicular separation.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[x + 2 y + z=11\]

(c)

\[\Sigma_1: x + 2 y + z=8\]
\[\Sigma_2: x + 2 y + z=14\]
\[d=\sqrt{6}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- \lambda + \mu - 3\\2 \lambda - \mu + 8\\- 3 \lambda + \mu - 7\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 2 \left(7 \lambda - 3 \mu + 20\right)=0\]
\[- 3 \left(2 \lambda - \mu + 6\right)=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=-2,\qquad\mu=2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

(b)

A normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), and the midpoint of \(PQ\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\\3\\\frac{7}{2}\end{pmatrix}\). Thus the plane is

\[x + 2 y + z=11\]

Expanding \(|\mathbf r-\mathbf p|^2=|\mathbf r-\mathbf q|^2\) gives the same equation, so every point of this plane is equidistant from \(P,Q\).

(c)

A plane parallel to \(\Pi\) has the same normal. The plane through each line uses its anchor to determine the constant. Since the line directions are perpendicular to \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), each whole line is contained. Their separation is

\[\frac{|6|}{\sqrt{6}}=\sqrt{6}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use two independent parameters and require the joining vector to have zero dot product with both directions.

(b)

Use the midpoint as an anchor and PQ as a normal; expand the squared distances for the justification.

(c)

Keep the normal fixed and determine each constant from its line anchor.

The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\-5\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

\[52-35\tau=-18\]
\[\tau=2\]

\[4 x - 3 y - 6 z=-11\]

(b)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}8\\-6\\-12\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\\-6\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\\-6\end{pmatrix}=-11\]

Using the point \(\left(-2,-5,3\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[4 x - 3 y - 6 z=-11\]

(b)

For plane \(\Pi_2\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}7\\-1\\-5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}13\\36\\11\end{pmatrix}\]

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\\-6\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}13\\36\\11\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[- 2 \left(7 \lambda - 4 \mu - 11\right)=0\]
\[- 2 \left(4 \lambda - 11 \mu - 15\right)=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=1,\qquad\mu=-1\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\4\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\-6\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

    [3]

  2. Find the position vector of \(H\), the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) to the plane.

    [4]

  3. Find a vector equation of the orthogonal projection of \(l\) onto \(\Pi\).

    [4]

  4. Find the acute angle between \(l\) and \(\Pi\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-5\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-3\\5\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-3\\5\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(a)

Substitute the line into the plane equation:

\[18+(13)\lambda=5\]

Since \(13\)\(\ne0\), there is exactly one intersection. Substitution into the line gives

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-5\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

Therefore

Project a general point \(\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w\) onto the plane. Removing the normal component gives

\[\mathbf h(\lambda)=\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w-\frac{\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w)-d}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n\]

Collect constant and parameter terms:

\[\mathbf h(\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-3\\5\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

The new direction is non-zero and has zero dot product with \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}\). Thus this is a line in the plane, not a single point. Equivalently, a direction is \((\mathbf n\times\mathbf w)\times\mathbf n\).

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|13|}{3 \sqrt{39}}=\frac{\sqrt{39}}{9}\]

questions.title: A plane fixed by a line and a perpendicular plane
questions.prompt_html:
The plane \(\Pi\) contains the line

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi\).

    [5]

  2. Find the position vector of \(H\), the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) to the plane. Give the exact perpendicular distance.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[12 x + 5 y + 11 z=48\]

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[d=2 \sqrt{290}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The required normal is perpendicular to the line direction \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and to the normal \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-5\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) of \(\Sigma\). Thus it is parallel to

\[\begin{pmatrix}-12\\-5\\-11\end{pmatrix}\]

Take \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\5\\11\end{pmatrix}\) and substitute \(\left(0,3,3\right)\), giving

\[12 x + 5 y + 11 z=48\]

(b)

The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\5\\11\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

\[628-290\tau=48\]
\[\tau=2\]

Therefore

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[d=|2|\sqrt{290}=2 \sqrt{290}\]

(a)

Its normal must be perpendicular to the given line direction and the other plane normal.

(b)

questions.title: Planes hinged on the common perpendicular
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\-6\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}7\\-2\\-6\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

Planes \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\) each contain the common perpendicular; they also contain \(l_1\) and \(l_2\), respectively.

  1. The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors. Hence give a vector equation of the common perpendicular.

    [7]

  2. Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi_2\).

    [4]

  3. Find the acute angle between \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\-4\\-6\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[x - y + z=3\]

(c)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{7}\right)=67.8^\circ\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- \lambda + \mu + 4\\3 \lambda + \mu - 2\\- 2 \lambda\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 2 \left(7 \lambda + \mu - 5\right)=0\]
\[2 \left(\lambda + \mu + 1\right)=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=1,\qquad\mu=-2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\-4\\-6\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

A line through \(P\) parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) is therefore

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}=3\]

Using the point \(\left(7,-2,-6\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[x - y + z=3\]

(c)

For plane \(\Pi_1\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}8\\4\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

For plane \(\Pi_2\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|3|}{3 \sqrt{7}}=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{7}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{7}\right)=67.8^\circ\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use two independent parameters and require the joining vector to have zero dot product with both directions.

(b)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(c)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

questions.title: A moving line and an exact distance condition
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}t - 3\\-4\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

Here \(t\) is real. Let \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=CD\).

  1. Find the value of \(t\) for which the two lines intersect, and find their point of intersection.

    [4]

  2. For this value of \(t\), find the plane containing the two lines.

    [4]

  3. Find all real values of \(t\) for which the shortest distance is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[t=- \frac{1}{2},\qquad \mathbf h=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[2 x - 3 y - 2 z=-1\]

(c)

\[t=- \frac{14}{11}\quad\text{or}\quad0\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The directions are never parallel. The lines intersect precisely when the connector has zero component along their common normal:

\[- 2 t - 1=0\]
\[t=- \frac{1}{2}\]

At this parameter, equate the coordinates of \(\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf u\) and \(\mathbf c+\mu\mathbf v\). The solution is

\[\lambda=1,\qquad\mu=-2\]
\[t=- \frac{1}{2},\qquad \mathbf h=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{1}{2}\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\- \frac{3}{2}\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}=-1\]

Using the point \(\left(-3,-1,-1\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[2 x - 3 y - 2 z=-1\]

(c)

The common normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\t - 1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\), so the distance formula gives

\[\frac{|- 2 t - 1|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 2 t + 3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\]

Both sides are non-negative and the denominator is strictly positive, so squaring introduces no additional sign condition:

\[\frac{t \left(11 t + 14\right)}{3}=0\]

Solving gives

\[t=- \frac{14}{11}\quad\text{or}\quad0\]

Substitution of each value in the original distance formula gives \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Both values are admissible.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The common-normal component must be zero; then verify the intersection by solving for the two line parameters.

(b)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(c)

Keep the absolute value until squaring, and check every candidate in the original distance condition.

Solve the line equations at this value.
Form two directions and their vector product.
Substitute a known point to obtain the constant.

  2. Find the exact perpendicular distance from \(D\) to \(ABC\).

    [3]

  3. Show that \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are skew, and find their exact shortest distance.

    [5]

(a)

\[2 x + 6 y - 5 z=-23\]

(b)

\[d=\sqrt{65}\]

(c)

\[d=\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-6\\5\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\6\\-5\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}2\\6\\-5\end{pmatrix}=-23\]

Using the point \(\left(4,-6,-1\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[2 x + 6 y - 5 z=-23\]

(b)

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\6\\-5\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|65|}{\sqrt{65}}=\sqrt{65}\]

The absolute value ensures a non-negative distance.

(c)

A common perpendicular direction is

\[\mathbf n=\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}24\\7\\5\end{pmatrix}\]

Project the connector between the two given anchors onto this normal:

\[d=\frac{|(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|65|}{5 \sqrt{26}}=\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2}\]

The vector product is non-zero and the scalar product is non-zero, so the lines are non-parallel and non-coplanar: they are skew.

questions.title: A family through an intersection line
questions.prompt_html:
The planes \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\) have equations

\[3 x + 2 z=-10\]

The family \(\Pi_k\) is defined by

\[3 k x + k y + 2 k z + 3 x + 2 z=- 10 \left(k + 1\right)\]

For part (c), use the positive value of \(k\) and point \(P=\left(2,2,5\right)\).

  1. Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).

    [4]

  2. Find all \(k\) for which \(\Pi_k\) makes equal acute angles with \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).

    [6]

  3. Find the exact perpendicular distance from \(P\) to \(\Pi_k\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{10}{3}\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[k=\pm \frac{\sqrt{182}}{14}\]

(c)

\[d=\frac{2 \left(\sqrt{91} + 7 \sqrt{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\sqrt{182} + 14}}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

A direction of the intersection is perpendicular to both normals:

\[\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence we may take direction \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). Solving the two plane equations with a convenient coordinate set to zero gives the point \(\left(- \frac{10}{3},0,0\right)\). It satisfies both equations:

\[-10=-10,\qquad -10=-10\]

The required line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{10}{3}\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

A common factor \(|\mathbf n_1+k\mathbf n_2|\) cancels from the equal-angle condition. The absolute dot products must satisfy

\[\frac{|13 \left(k + 1\right)|}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{|14 k + 13|}{\sqrt{14}}\]

Squaring and simplifying gives

\[- 13 \left(14 k^{2} - 13\right)=0\]
\[k=\pm \frac{\sqrt{182}}{14}\]

The normals of the original planes are independent, so the family normal never vanishes. Both signs satisfy the original absolute-value equation.

(c)

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{3 \left(\sqrt{182} + 14\right)}{14}\\\frac{\sqrt{182}}{14}\\\frac{\sqrt{182} + 14}{7}\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|2 \left(13 + \sqrt{182}\right)|}{\frac{\sqrt{91} \sqrt{\sqrt{182} + 14}}{7}}=\frac{2 \left(\sqrt{91} + 7 \sqrt{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\sqrt{182} + 14}}\]

The absolute value ensures a non-negative distance.

(b)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{10}{3}\\\frac{1}{3}\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]

\[d=\sqrt{10}\]

(a)

A direction of the intersection is perpendicular to both normals:

questions.title: A shortest route constrained to touch a plane
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\5\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\9\\4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\5\\11\end{pmatrix}\]

Let \(\Pi\) be the plane \(ABC\). A point \(X\) may be chosen anywhere in \(\Pi\).

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi\).

    [4]

  2. Find the position vector of \(H\), the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) to the plane. Hence find the reflection \(R\) of \(P\) in the plane.

    [4]

  3. Find the minimum possible value of \(PX+XQ\) and the position of \(X\) where it is attained. Justify that your value is a global minimum.

    [7]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[2 y + 3 z=4\]

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\5\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OR}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\-8\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\min(PX+XQ)=\sqrt{377}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\\frac{13}{5}\\- \frac{2}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-8\\-12\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}=4\]

Using the point \(\left(2,2,0\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[2 y + 3 z=4\]

(b)

The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

\[30-13\tau=4\]
\[\tau=2\]

Therefore

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\5\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

The foot is the midpoint of the original point and its reflection:

\[\mathbf r=2\mathbf h-\mathbf p=\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\-8\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

The two points are on the same side of the plane because their signed normal displacements are \(2|\mathbf n|\) and \(3|\mathbf n|\). Reflect \(P\) to \(R=\left(4,1,-8\right)\). For every point \(X\) of the plane, \(PX=RX\). Therefore the triangle inequality gives

\[PX+XQ=RX+XQ\geq RQ=\sqrt{377}\]

Equality holds exactly when \(X\) lies on segment \(RQ\). On that segment write \(\mathbf x=\mathbf r+\tau(\mathbf q-\mathbf r)\). The signed normal component is proportional to \(-2+5\tau\), so \(\tau=2/5\). Thus

\[\mathbf x=\frac35\begin{pmatrix}4\\5\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\frac25\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\\frac{13}{5}\\- \frac{2}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]

Since \(0<2/5<1\), this is on the segment and attains the lower bound.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(b)

The perpendicular direction is the plane normal. A reflection uses the foot as the midpoint.

(c)

Reflect one endpoint, and use the triangle inequality for a straight segment through the plane.

questions.prompt_html:
Two vectors are \(\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}\). A vector \(\mathbf w\) is perpendicular to both, has magnitude 3 and has positive x-component. The point \(A\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Calculate \(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(\mathbf w\).

    [3]

\[\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

\[\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{3 \sqrt{14}}{7}\\\frac{9 \sqrt{14}}{14}\\- \frac{3 \sqrt{14}}{14}\end{pmatrix}\]

\[\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Every common perpendicular is parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\). Use \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) with the required sign and rescale it:

\[\mathbf w=\frac3{\sqrt{14}}\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{3 \sqrt{14}}{7}\\\frac{9 \sqrt{14}}{14}\\- \frac{3 \sqrt{14}}{14}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}=7\]

Using the point \(\left(0,3,2\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[2 x + 3 y - z=7\]

questions.title: A parallel line and a crossing plane
questions.prompt_html:
The plane \(\Pi_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

The parameters \(s\) and \(t\) are real.

The line \(l\) and a second plane \(\Pi_2\) are

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[2 x + 3 y + z=8\]

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi_1\).

    [4]

  2. Show that \(l\) is parallel to, but not contained in, \(\Pi_1\).

    [2]

  3. Find the exact perpendicular distance from \(l\) to \(\Pi_1\).

    [3]

  4. Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[2 y - z=-1\]

(b)

\(l\) is parallel to, but does not lie in, \(\Pi_1\).

(c)

\[d=\sqrt{5}\]

(d)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{19}{4}\\- \frac{1}{2}\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}5\\-2\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-4\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}=-1\]

Using the point \(\left(1,0,1\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[2 y - z=-1\]

(b)

\[\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n=0\]

The direction is parallel to the plane. However the given point on the line has \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf n=4\), not \(-1\). Thus there is no intersection and the line is not contained in the plane.

(c)

Every point of the parallel line has the same plane distance; use its given anchor \(\left(1,2,0\right)\).

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|5|}{\sqrt{5}}=\sqrt{5}\]

The absolute value ensures a non-negative distance.

(d)

A direction of the intersection is perpendicular to both normals:

\[\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2=\begin{pmatrix}5\\-2\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence we may take direction \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\-2\\-4\end{pmatrix}\). Solving the two plane equations with a convenient coordinate set to zero gives the point \(\left(\frac{19}{4},- \frac{1}{2},0\right)\). It satisfies both equations:

\[-1=-1,\qquad 8=8\]

The required line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{19}{4}\\- \frac{1}{2}\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}5\\-2\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]

(a)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(b)

Check both the direction and a point; a zero dot product alone does not distinguish the two cases.

(c)

Divide the absolute residual in the plane equation by the length of its normal.

(d)

Cross the two normals for the direction, then find one point satisfying both plane equations.

questions.title: A bisector plane between skew lines
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\\5\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\6\\4\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

The common perpendicular meets the lines at \(P\) and \(Q\). Let \(\Pi\) be the perpendicular bisector plane of \(PQ\).

  1. The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors.

    [6]

  2. Find the equation of \(\Pi\) and explain why its points are equidistant from \(P\) and \(Q\).

    [4]

  3. Find a vector equation of the reflection of \(l_1\) in the plane, explaining how its direction is obtained.

    [3]

  4. Determine whether the reflected image of \(l_1\) intersects \(l_2\). Justify your answer.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\4\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[y - z=1\]

(c)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\6\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

(d)

They intersect at \(Q=\left(3,5,3\right)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- 2 \left(\lambda - 1\right)\\\lambda + \mu + 1\\\lambda + \mu - 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 2 \left(3 \lambda + \mu - 2\right)=0\]
\[2 \left(\lambda + \mu\right)=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=1,\qquad\mu=-1\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\4\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

(b)

A normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\), and the midpoint of \(PQ\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\\frac{9}{2}\\\frac{7}{2}\end{pmatrix}\). Thus the plane is

\[y - z=1\]

Expanding \(|\mathbf r-\mathbf p|^2=|\mathbf r-\mathbf q|^2\) gives the same equation, so every point of this plane is equidistant from \(P,Q\).

(c)

For any point \(\mathbf x\), its reflection in the plane is

\[\mathbf x^*=\mathbf x-2\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf x-d}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n\]

Insert \(\mathbf x=\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w\) and collect the constant and parameter terms:

\[\mathbf p^*=\begin{pmatrix}1\\6\\4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf w^*=\mathbf w-2\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf w}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence the image line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\6\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

(d)

Reflection sends \(P\) to \(Q\) and leaves the direction \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) unchanged, since it is parallel to the mirror plane. The image line therefore passes through \(Q\). Its direction is not parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\), so the intersection is unique.

(a)

Use two independent parameters and require the joining vector to have zero dot product with both directions.

(b)

Use the midpoint as an anchor and PQ as a normal; expand the squared distances for the justification.

(c)

(d)

Track the reflected foot and compare the two directions.

questions.title: A family with contained, parallel and crossing cases
questions.prompt_html:
For each real \(t\), a line \(l_t\) has equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}t - 3\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}t^{2} - 3 t + 3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

The fixed plane \(\Pi\) has equation

\[x + 3 y - z=-2\]

  1. Classify the position of \(l_t\) relative to \(\Pi\) for every real \(t\).

    [5]

  2. Find the unique intersection in terms of \(t\), stating the parameter restrictions.

    [4]

  3. Describe exactly the locus of the unique intersection points, including any omitted points.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(t=0\): the entire line lies in \(\Pi\). \(t=3\): parallel and disjoint. All other real values: a unique intersection.

(b)

\[\lambda=-\frac1{t-3},\qquad \mathbf x=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{3 \left(t - 2\right)}{t - 3}\\\frac{1}{t - 3}\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

Exclude \(\left(-3,0,-1\right)\) and \(\left(-2,- \frac{1}{3},-1\right)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Substitution into the plane equation gives

\[t \left(\lambda t - 3 \lambda + 1\right)=0\]

If \(t=0\), this is true for every \(\lambda\), so the line is contained. If \(t=3\), the left side is the non-zero constant \(3\), so there is no intersection. Otherwise it gives exactly one value of \(\lambda\).

(b)

For \(t\ne 0,3\), division is valid. Thus \(\lambda=-1/(t-3)\). Inserting it into the line cancels the component in \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and leaves

\[\mathbf x=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}-\frac1{t-3}\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Put \(s=-1/(t-3)\). As \(t\) varies, \(s\) takes every real value except zero and \(\frac{1}{3}\). Zero is never attained; the second excluded value would require the contained-line case \(t=0\). The converse \(t=3-1/s\) shows there are no other omissions.
questions.hint_html:
(a)
