questions.title: Two independent geometric parameter conditions
questions.prompt_html:
The plane \(\Pi_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]

The parameters \(s\) and \(t\) are real.

Plane \(\Pi_2\) has equation \(5 x + y=7\). A point \(P\) and line direction \(\mathbf w\) are defined by

\[\mathbf p=\begin{pmatrix}3 a - 10\\2 a - 5\\2 \left(a - 1\right)\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}3 b + 2\\2 b - 1\\2 \left(b - 1\right)\end{pmatrix}\]

The constants \(a\) and \(b\) are positive.

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi_1\).

    [3]

  2. Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).

    [4]

  3. Find every possible \(a\) for which the distance of \(P\) from \(\Pi_1\) is \(\sqrt{17}\).

    [3]

  4. The line through \(P\) in direction \(\mathbf w\) makes an acute angle of 45° with \(\Pi_1\). Find \(b\) exactly.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[3 x + 2 y + 2 z=7\]

(b)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-10\\7\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[a=2\quad\text{or}\quad4\]

(d)

\[b=\frac{3 \sqrt{17}}{17}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}=7\]

Using the point \(\left(-1,2,3\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[3 x + 2 y + 2 z=7\]

(b)

A direction of the intersection is perpendicular to both normals:

\[\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\10\\-7\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence we may take direction \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-10\\7\end{pmatrix}\). Solving the two plane equations with a convenient coordinate set to zero gives the point \(\left(1,2,0\right)\). It satisfies both equations:

\[7=7,\qquad 7=7\]

The required line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-10\\7\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Substitution in the plane equation gives signed residual \(17 \left(a - 3\right)\). Therefore

\[\operatorname{dist}(P,\Pi_1)=|a-3|\sqrt{17}\]

Equating this to \(\sqrt{17}\) gives \(a=2\text{ or }a=4\). Retain only the positive values:

\[a=2\quad\text{or}\quad4\]

(d)

Since \(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n=0\), the line direction has squared length \(17 b^{2} + 9\). For a 45° line–plane angle,

\[\frac{b|\mathbf n|}{\sqrt{|\mathbf u|^2+b^2|\mathbf n|^2}}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\]

Squaring and simplifying gives \(17 b^{2}\)=\(9\). Positivity selects

\[b=\frac{3 \sqrt{17}}{17}\]

(a)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(b)

Cross the two normals for the direction, then find one point satisfying both plane equations.

(c)

Solve the absolute-value equation, then enforce positivity.

(d)

Use sine for the line–plane angle and the orthogonality of u and n.

questions.title: Equal-distance loci in three dimensions
questions.prompt_html:
Two planes are given by

\[\Pi_1: x + 2 y + 2 z=5\]
\[\Pi_2: 2 x + 2 y - z=-2\]

Point \(P_\lambda\) moves on the line

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

  1. Find the acute angle between \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]

  2. Show that points equidistant from the two planes lie on one of two planes, and find their equations.

    [5]

  3. Find all values of \(\lambda\) for which \(P_\lambda\) is equidistant from \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).

    [4]

(a)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)=63.6^\circ\]

(b)

\[- x + 3 z=7\]
\[3 x + 4 y + z=3\]

(c)

\[\lambda=5\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{7}{11}\]

(a)

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|4|}{9}=\frac{4}{9}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)=63.6^\circ\]

(b)

Both normals have length 3. Equal perpendicular distances are therefore equivalent to

\[|x + 2 y + 2 z - 5|=|2 x + 2 y - z + 2|\]

The quantities inside the moduli are either equal or negatives. These give the two planes

\[- x + 3 z=7\]
\[3 x + 4 y + z=3\]

(c)

Substitute the moving point into each bisector plane:

\[\lambda - 5=0\]
\[11 \lambda - 7=0\]
\[\lambda=5\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{7}{11}\]

(a)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

(b)

Equate the distances with absolute values, keeping both signs.

(c)

Intersect the given line with each of the two bisector planes.

Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-10\\4\\3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-7\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of \(ABC\).

    [4]

  2. Find the exact perpendicular distance from \(O\) to \(ABC\).

    [3]

  3. The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors. Hence give a vector equation of the common perpendicular.

(a)

\[z=3\]

(b)

\[d=3\]

(c)

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{11}{7}\\- \frac{34}{21}\\3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\\frac{31}{42}\\\frac{31}{14}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{11}{7}\\- \frac{34}{21}\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\11\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}=3\]

Using the point \(\left(-10,4,3\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[z=3\]

(b)

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|-3|}{1}=3\]

The absolute value ensures a non-negative distance.

(c)

Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}10 - 3 \lambda\\2 \lambda + \mu - 4\\3 \left(\mu - 1\right)\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 13 \lambda - 2 \mu + 38=0\]
\[2 \lambda + 10 \mu - 13=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=\frac{59}{21},\qquad\mu=\frac{31}{42}\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{11}{7}\\- \frac{34}{21}\\3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\\frac{31}{42}\\\frac{31}{14}\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{11}{7}\\\frac{33}{14}\\- \frac{11}{14}\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

A line through \(P\) parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) is therefore

questions.title: A family with contained, parallel and crossing cases
questions.prompt_html:
For each real \(t\), a line \(l_t\) has equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}t\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}t^{2} - 3 t + 3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

The fixed plane \(\Pi\) has equation

\[x + 3 y - z=-6\]

In part (d), use \(t=4\).

  1. Classify the position of \(l_t\) relative to \(\Pi\) for every real \(t\).

    [5]

  2. Find the unique intersection in terms of \(t\), stating the parameter restrictions.

    [4]

  3. Describe exactly the locus of the unique intersection points, including any omitted points.

    [4]

  4. Find the acute angle between \(l_{4}\) and \(\Pi\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(t=0\): the entire line lies in \(\Pi\). \(t=3\): parallel and disjoint. All other real values: a unique intersection.

(b)

\[\lambda=-\frac1{t-3},\qquad \mathbf x=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{3}{t - 3}\\- \frac{2 t - 7}{t - 3}\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

Exclude \(\left(0,-2,0\right)\) and \(\left(1,- \frac{7}{3},0\right)\).

(d)

\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{22}}{55}\right)=9.8^\circ\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Substitution into the plane equation gives

\[t \left(\lambda t - 3 \lambda + 1\right)=0\]

If \(t=0\), this is true for every \(\lambda\), so the line is contained. If \(t=3\), the left side is the non-zero constant \(3\), so there is no intersection. Otherwise it gives exactly one value of \(\lambda\).

(b)

For \(t\ne 0,3\), division is valid. Thus \(\lambda=-1/(t-3)\). Inserting it into the line cancels the component in \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and leaves

\[\mathbf x=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}-\frac1{t-3}\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Put \(s=-1/(t-3)\). As \(t\) varies, \(s\) takes every real value except zero and \(\frac{1}{3}\). Zero is never attained; the second excluded value would require the contained-line case \(t=0\). The converse \(t=3-1/s\) shows there are no other omissions.

(d)

Use the line direction and plane normal:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}7\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

The angle between a line and a plane is the complement of the angle between its direction and the plane normal. Therefore use sine, not cosine.

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|4|}{5 \sqrt{22}}=\frac{2 \sqrt{22}}{55}\]
\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{22}}{55}\right)=9.8^\circ\]

(a)

(b)

(c)

Reparameterise the intersection and track which parameter values are unavailable.

(d)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-3\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\1\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\2\\t - 4\end{pmatrix}\]

Here \(t\) is real. Let \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=CD\).

  1. Find the shortest distance between \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) as a function of \(t\).

    [4]

  2. Find all real values of \(t\) for which the shortest distance is \(\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{3}\).

    [4]

  3. Let \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\) be the planes \(ABD\) for \(t=\frac{23}{11}\) and \(t=3\), respectively. Find their Cartesian equations.

    [4]

  4. Find the acute angle between \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]

  5. Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[d(t)=\frac{|- t - 2|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 4 t + 6}}\]

(b)

\[t=\frac{23}{11}\quad\text{or}\quad3\]

(c)

\[\Pi_1: 43 x + 22 y - 22 z=-172\]
\[\Pi_2: 3 x + 2 y - 2 z=-12\]

(d)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{217 \sqrt{5321}}{15963}\right)=7.4^\circ\]

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(a)

The line directions have vector product

\[\mathbf n(t)=\begin{pmatrix}t - 2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

This vector never vanishes. The anchor connector has scalar product \(- t - 2\) with it, so the perpendicular separation is

\[d(t)=\frac{|- t - 2|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 4 t + 6}}\]

A zero numerator corresponds to intersecting, not skew, lines; the same expression then gives distance zero.

(b)

Use the distance expression obtained above.

\[\frac{|- t - 2|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 4 t + 6}}=\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{3}\]

Both sides are non-negative and the denominator is strictly positive, so squaring introduces no additional sign condition:

\[- \frac{2 \left(t - 3\right) \left(11 t - 23\right)}{3}=0\]

Solving gives

\[t=\frac{23}{11}\quad\text{or}\quad3\]

Substitution of each value in the original distance formula gives \(\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{3}\). Both values are admissible.

(c)

For \(t=\frac{23}{11}\), \(D=\left(-6,2,- \frac{21}{11}\right)\). A normal to \(ABD\) is

\[\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AD}=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{43}{11}\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}43\\22\\-22\end{pmatrix}\) and point \(\left(-4,-3,-3\right)\).

\[43 x + 22 y - 22 z=-172\]

For \(t=3\), \(D=\left(-6,2,-1\right)\). A normal to \(ABD\) is

Use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and point \(\left(-4,-3,-3\right)\).

\[3 x + 2 y - 2 z=-12\]

(d)

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}43\\22\\-22\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|217|}{3 \sqrt{5321}}=\frac{217 \sqrt{5321}}{15963}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{217 \sqrt{5321}}{15963}\right)=7.4^\circ\]

\[\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2=\begin{pmatrix}0\\20\\20\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence we may take direction \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Solving the two plane equations with a convenient coordinate set to zero gives the point \(\left(-4,0,0\right)\). It satisfies both equations:

\[-172=-172,\qquad -12=-12\]

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

questions.title: A plane specified by two intersecting lines
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\6\\1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

The two lines lie in \(\Pi\). Point \(P\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}9\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\). The line \(m\) through \(P\) has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi\).

    [4]

  2. Find the acute angle between \(m\) and \(\Pi\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]

  3. Find the position vector of \(H\), the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) to the plane.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[3 x + 2 y - 2 z=1\]

(b)

\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{510}}{30}\right)=48.8^\circ\]

(c)

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}=1\]

Using the point \(\left(-3,6,1\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[3 x + 2 y - 2 z=1\]

(b)

Use the line direction and plane normal:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}5\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

The angle between a line and a plane is the complement of the angle between its direction and the plane normal. Therefore use sine, not cosine.

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|17|}{\sqrt{510}}=\frac{\sqrt{510}}{30}\]
\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{510}}{30}\right)=48.8^\circ\]

(c)

The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

\[35-17\tau=1\]
\[\tau=2\]

Therefore

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(b)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

(c)

The perpendicular direction is the plane normal. A reflection uses the foot as the midpoint.

questions.title: Recover the mirror plane from two points
questions.prompt_html:
Reflection in an unknown plane \(\Pi\) maps \(P=\left(6,6,0\right)\) to \(R=\left(-2,4,-4\right)\). A line \(l\) has equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}6\\6\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of the reflecting plane.

    [4]

  2. Find the position vector of \(H\), the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) to the plane.

    [2]

  3. Find a vector equation of the reflection of \(l\) in the plane, explaining how its direction is obtained.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[4 x + y + 2 z=9\]

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\4\\-4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The mirror plane is the perpendicular bisector of \(PR\). It contains midpoint \(\left(2,5,-2\right)\) and has normal parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}8\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}\). Taking the simpler normal \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\) gives

\[4 x + y + 2 z=9\]

(b)

The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

\[30-21\tau=9\]
\[\tau=1\]

Therefore

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

For any point \(\mathbf x\), its reflection in the plane is

\[\mathbf x^*=\mathbf x-2\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf x-d}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n\]

Insert \(\mathbf x=\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w\) and collect the constant and parameter terms:

\[\mathbf p^*=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\4\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf w^*=\mathbf w-2\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf w}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence the image line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\4\\-4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the midpoint of PR and a normal in direction PR.

(b)

The perpendicular direction is the plane normal. A reflection uses the foot as the midpoint.

(c)

Reflect a general point on the line, not only the anchor.

questions.title: Recovering a direction from two planes
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l\) passes through \(P\) with position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\p\\q\end{pmatrix}\). It is parallel to both planes

\[x + 2 y - z=5\]
\[2 x - y + 3 z=-2\]

A third plane \(\Pi\) has equation

\[x + y + z=4\]

  1. Determine \(p\) and \(q\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(X\), the point where \(l\) meets \(\Pi\).

    [3]

  3. Find the exact shortest distance from \(O\) to \(l\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[p=-1,\quad q=-1\]

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[d=\frac{\sqrt{78}}{3}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

A direction parallel to a plane is perpendicular to its normal. Therefore

\[1+2p-q=0,\qquad 2-p+3q=0\]

From the first equation q = 1 + 2p. Substitute into the second to obtain 5 + 5p = 0, so

\[p=-1,\quad q=-1\]

Thus a direction of the line is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\).

(b)

Substitute the line into the plane equation:

\[2+(-1)\lambda=4\]
\[\lambda=-2\]

Since \(-1\)\(\ne0\), there is exactly one intersection. Substitution into the line gives

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Project \(\mathbf p-\mathbf a\) onto the line direction. The foot has parameter

\[\tau=\frac{(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}=- \frac{4}{3}\]
\[\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\tau\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{5}{3}\\- \frac{2}{3}\\\frac{7}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

Therefore the perpendicular distance is

\[|\mathbf p-\mathbf h|=\frac{\sqrt{78}}{3}\]

Equivalently, use \(|(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf u|/|\mathbf u|\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the two normal vectors to form simultaneous equations.

(b)

Insert the line coordinates into the plane equation, solve for the parameter, then substitute back.

(c)

Find the foot by a scalar product, or use the magnitude of a vector product divided by the direction length.

questions.title: The angle between two perpendicular-supporting planes
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}7\\0\\11\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

Plane \(\Pi_1\) contains \(l_1\) and the common perpendicular. Plane \(\Pi_2\) contains \(l_2\) and the common perpendicular.

  1. Show that \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are skew, and find their exact shortest distance.

    [5]

  2. Give a vector equation of \(\Pi_1\) in two-parameter form.

    [3]

  3. Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi_2\).

    [4]

  4. Find the acute angle between \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[d=\sqrt{66}\]

(b)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\-7\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[29 x - 5 y - 16 z=27\]

(d)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{187}}{17}\right)=36.4^\circ\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

A common perpendicular direction is

\[\mathbf n=\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-7\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

Project the connector between the two given anchors onto this normal:

\[d=\frac{|(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|66|}{\sqrt{66}}=\sqrt{66}\]

The vector product is non-zero and the scalar product is non-zero, so the lines are non-parallel and non-coplanar: they are skew.

(b)

Use the known point \(\left(-1,2,0\right)\). The independent directions \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-7\\4\end{pmatrix}\) are parallel to the plane; their cross product is non-zero. Therefore

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\-7\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-7\\4\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}29\\-5\\-16\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}29\\-5\\-16\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}29\\-5\\-16\end{pmatrix}=27\]

Using the point \(\left(7,0,11\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[29 x - 5 y - 16 z=27\]

(d)

For plane \(\Pi_1\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}1\\-7\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}11\\-11\\-22\end{pmatrix}\]

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

For plane \(\Pi_2\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}1\\-7\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}29\\-5\\-16\end{pmatrix}\]

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}29\\-5\\-16\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|66|}{6 \sqrt{187}}=\frac{\sqrt{187}}{17}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{187}}{17}\right)=36.4^\circ\]

Find a vector perpendicular to both directions, and project a joining vector onto it.

(b)

A plane needs an anchor and two non-parallel directions.

(c)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

questions.title: A cross-product equation with a geometric conclusion
questions.prompt_html:
The non-zero vector \(\mathbf u\) and vector \(\mathbf b\) are

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-6\\-6\end{pmatrix}\]

A vector \(\mathbf w\) satisfies \(\mathbf w\times\mathbf u=\mathbf b\).

For parts (d) and (e), use the unique vector found in (c). Point \(A\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) and point \(P\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Verify the necessary condition \(\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf u=0\).

    [2]

  2. Find all vectors \(\mathbf w\) satisfying the cross-product equation.

    [5]

  3. Given additionally \(\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf u=33\), find \(\mathbf w\).

    [2]

  4. Find the equation of the plane \(\Pi\) through \(A\) perpendicular to \(\mathbf w\).

    [3]

  5. Find the exact perpendicular distance from \(P\) to \(\Pi\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf u=0\]

(b)

\[\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\quad\lambda\in\mathbb R\]

(c)

\[\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}9\\-1\\-5\end{pmatrix}\]

(d)

\[9 x - y - 5 z=21\]

(e)

\[d=\frac{33 \sqrt{107}}{107}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-6\\-6\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}=0\]

A vector product is perpendicular to each of its factors.

(b)

Writing \(\mathbf w=(X,Y,Z)^T\) gives the component equations

\[- Y + Z + 4=0\]
\[X + 3 Z + 6=0\]
\[- X - 3 Y + 6=0\]

One solution, obtained by substitution, is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). If w is any other solution, subtracting their vector equations gives

\[(\mathbf w-\mathbf w_0)\times\mathbf u=\mathbf0\]

Since u is non-zero, w − w₀ is parallel to u. Conversely, adding any scalar multiple of u does not change the cross product. Therefore all solutions are

\[\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\quad\lambda\in\mathbb R\]

(c)

\[11+11\lambda=33\]
\[\lambda=2\]
\[\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}9\\-1\\-5\end{pmatrix}\]

(d)

The plane passes through A and has normal w, hence

\[(\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf w=0\]
\[9 x - y - 5 z=21\]

(e)

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}9\\-1\\-5\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|33|}{\sqrt{107}}=\frac{33 \sqrt{107}}{107}\]

The absolute value ensures a non-negative distance.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

A cross product is perpendicular to both input vectors.

(b)

Write component equations; the difference of two solutions is parallel to u.

(c)

Use the scalar product to fix the remaining parameter.

(d)

Use w as the normal and A as an anchor.

(e)

Divide the absolute residual in the plane equation by the length of its normal.

questions.title: Equal-distance loci in three dimensions
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

The locus of points equidistant from \(A\) and \(B\) is a plane \(\Pi\). A line \(l\) is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

  1. Derive an equation of \(\Pi\) from the equal-distance condition.

    [4]

  2. Find \(X\), the point where \(l\) meets \(\Pi\).

    [4]

  3. Find the acute angle between \(l\) and \(\Pi\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[x + y=-2\]

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)=45.0^\circ\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For a point with position vector \(\mathbf r\), expand \(|\mathbf r-\mathbf a|^2=|\mathbf r-\mathbf b|^2\). The quadratic terms cancel:

\[2\mathbf r\cdot(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=|\mathbf b|^2-|\mathbf a|^2\]

Equivalently, the plane passes through midpoint \(\left(-3,1,2\right)\) with normal \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\). Hence

\[x + y=-2\]

(b)

Substitute the line into the plane equation:

\[-2+(2)\lambda=-2\]
\[\lambda=0\]

Since \(2\)\(\ne0\), there is exactly one intersection. Substitution into the line gives

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Use the line direction and plane normal:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

The angle between a line and a plane is the complement of the angle between its direction and the plane normal. Therefore use sine, not cosine.

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|2|}{2 \sqrt{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\]
\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)=45.0^\circ\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the squares of the two distances and cancel the quadratic terms.

(b)

Insert the line coordinates into the plane equation, solve for the parameter, then substitute back.

(c)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

questions.title: Two support planes and an orthogonal projection
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

Point \(C\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\5\end{pmatrix}\). Plane \(\Pi_1\) contains \(l_1\) and \(C\). Plane \(\Pi_2\) contains \(l_2\) and is parallel to \(l_1\). Point \(P\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}7\\2\\11\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Give a vector equation of \(\Pi_1\) in two-parameter form.

    [3]

  2. Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi_2\).

    [4]

  3. Find the acute angle between \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]

  4. Find the position vector of \(H\), the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) to \(\Pi_2\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[2 x + 3 z=21\]

(c)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{38}}{19}\right)=49.5^\circ\]

(d)

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\5\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Use the known point \(\left(-2,1,4\right)\). The independent directions \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\) are parallel to the plane; their cross product is non-zero. Therefore

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-8\\0\\-12\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}=21\]

Using the point \(\left(6,-1,3\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[2 x + 3 z=21\]

(c)

For plane \(\Pi_1\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-13\\18\end{pmatrix}\]

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}1\\13\\-18\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|-52|}{13 \sqrt{38}}=\frac{2 \sqrt{38}}{19}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{38}}{19}\right)=49.5^\circ\]

(d)

The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

\[47-13\tau=21\]
\[\tau=2\]

Therefore

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\5\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

A plane needs an anchor and two non-parallel directions.

(b)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(c)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

(d)

The perpendicular direction is the plane normal. A reflection uses the foot as the midpoint.

Point \(P\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}-9\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), and the line \(l\) is

  3. Find the acute angle between \(l\) and \(\Pi\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]

  4. Find the exact perpendicular distance from \(P\) to \(\Pi\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[3 x - 2 y + 2 z=13\]

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-6\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{510}}{30}\right)=48.8^\circ\]

(d)

\[d=2 \sqrt{17}\]

(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}=13\]

Using the point \(\left(-1,-4,4\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[3 x - 2 y + 2 z=13\]

(b)

Substitute the line into the plane equation:

\[-21+(17)\lambda=13\]
\[\lambda=2\]

Since \(17\)\(\ne0\), there is exactly one intersection. Substitution into the line gives

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-6\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Use the line direction and plane normal:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}5\\-2\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

The angle between a line and a plane is the complement of the angle between its direction and the plane normal. Therefore use sine, not cosine.

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|17|}{\sqrt{510}}=\frac{\sqrt{510}}{30}\]
\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{510}}{30}\right)=48.8^\circ\]

(d)

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|-34|}{\sqrt{17}}=2 \sqrt{17}\]

questions.title: Parallel lines have many closest pairs
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}9\\-7\\-14\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}2\\-4\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

Here \(B\) denotes the anchor of \(l_2\).

  1. Explain why the two lines are distinct and parallel, and find their distance.

    [3]

  2. Find the position vector of the foot of the perpendicular from \(B\) to \(l_1\).

    [3]

  3. Give all pairs of points \(P\in l_1\), \(Q\in l_2\) for which \(PQ\) is a shortest joining segment.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The lines are distinct and parallel. Their distance is \(3 \sqrt{30}\).

(b)

\[d=3 \sqrt{30}\]
\[\mathbf h=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\mathbf p=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf q=\begin{pmatrix}9\\-7\\-14\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad s\in\mathbb R\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The directions \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-4\\2\end{pmatrix}\) are parallel. But \((\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}-36\\-18\\0\end{pmatrix}\)\(\ne\mathbf0\), so the lines are not coincident. The common-normal formula for skew lines would divide by zero; instead use the point-to-line distance

\[d=\frac{|(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf u|}{|\mathbf u|}=3 \sqrt{30}\]

(b)

Project \(\mathbf p-\mathbf a\) onto the line direction. The foot has parameter

\[\tau=\frac{(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}=2\]
\[\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\tau\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

Therefore the perpendicular distance is

\[|\mathbf p-\mathbf h|=3 \sqrt{30}\]

Equivalently, use \(|(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf u|/|\mathbf u|\).

(c)

Translate both feet by the same vector \(s\mathbf u\). The connector stays equal to \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-6\\-15\end{pmatrix}\), perpendicular to both lines, and has the required distance. Conversely the zero dot-product condition forces equal displacements along the common direction.

\[\mathbf p=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf q=\begin{pmatrix}9\\-7\\-14\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad s\in\mathbb R\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

For parallel lines, use the distance from one anchor to the other line.

(b)

Find the foot by a scalar product, or use the magnitude of a vector product divided by the direction length.

(c)

Unlike skew lines, distinct parallel lines have infinitely many shortest joining segments.

State the position vector of the perpendicular foot.

Explain why these give every closest pair.

questions.title: Planes through the origin and a skew-line connector
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

The plane \(\Pi\) has equation \(2 \left(2 x + y - z\right)=7\). Let \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=OC\).

  1. Find the plane \(OAB\) in scalar-product form and in Cartesian form.

    [4]

  2. Find the exact perpendicular distance from \(O\) to \(\Pi\).

    [3]

  3. Find the acute angle between \(OAB\) and \(\Pi\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]

  4. The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors. Hence give a vector equation of the common perpendicular.

    [7]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[3 x + 2 y + z=0\]
\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}=0\]

(b)

\[d=\frac{7 \sqrt{6}}{12}\]

(c)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{21}}{6}\right)=40.2^\circ\]

(d)

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{33}{35}\\-3\\\frac{111}{35}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{12}{7}\\- \frac{12}{7}\\\frac{24}{7}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{33}{35}\\-3\\\frac{111}{35}\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}9\\6\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}=0\]

Using the point \(\left(0,0,0\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[3 x + 2 y + z=0\]

(b)

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|-7|}{2 \sqrt{6}}=\frac{7 \sqrt{6}}{12}\]

The absolute value ensures a non-negative distance.

(c)

A normal to \(OAB\) is \(\overrightarrow{OA}\times\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}9\\6\\3\end{pmatrix}\).

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|14|}{4 \sqrt{21}}=\frac{\sqrt{21}}{6}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{21}}{6}\right)=40.2^\circ\]

(d)

Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- \lambda + \mu - 1\\3 - \mu\\3 \lambda + 2 \mu - 3\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 10 \lambda - 5 \mu + 8=0\]
\[5 \lambda + 6 \mu - 10=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=- \frac{2}{35},\qquad\mu=\frac{12}{7}\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{33}{35}\\-3\\\frac{111}{35}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{12}{7}\\- \frac{12}{7}\\\frac{24}{7}\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{27}{35}\\\frac{9}{7}\\\frac{9}{35}\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

A line through \(P\) parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\\1\end{pmatrix}\) is therefore

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{33}{35}\\-3\\\frac{111}{35}\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(a)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(b)

Divide the absolute residual in the plane equation by the length of its normal.

(c)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

(d)

Use two independent parameters and require the joining vector to have zero dot product with both directions.

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}17\\16\\7\end{pmatrix}=-20\]

Using the point \(\left(-6,6,-2\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[17 x + 16 y + 7 z=-20\]

(c)

Use the line direction and plane normal:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}17\\16\\7\end{pmatrix}\]

questions.title: Skew sides and a triangular plane
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\6\\-5\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\4\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\4\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

The lines are \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=CD\).

  1. Show that \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are skew, and find their exact shortest distance.

    [5]

  2. Find the acute angle between \(CD\) and \(ABD\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[d=\sqrt{2}\]

(b)

\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7}\right)=32.3^\circ\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

A common perpendicular direction is

\[\mathbf n=\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

Project the connector between the two given anchors onto this normal:

\[d=\frac{|(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|-2|}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}\]

The vector product is non-zero and the scalar product is non-zero, so the lines are non-parallel and non-coplanar: they are skew.

(b)

For plane \(ABD\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

Use the line direction and plane normal:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

The angle between a line and a plane is the complement of the angle between its direction and the plane normal. Therefore use sine, not cosine.

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|2|}{\sqrt{14}}=\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7}\]
\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7}\right)=32.3^\circ\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Find a vector perpendicular to both directions, and project a joining vector onto it.

(b)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

questions.title: A moving line and an exact distance condition
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\t + 1\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]

Here \(t\) is real. Let \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=CD\).

  1. Find the value of \(t\) for which the two lines intersect, and find their point of intersection.

    [4]

  2. For this value of \(t\), find the plane containing the two lines.

    [4]

  3. Find all real values of \(t\) for which the shortest distance is \(\sqrt{3}\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[t=\frac{1}{2},\qquad \mathbf h=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[2 x + 2 y - z=-2\]

(c)

\[t=-1\quad\text{or}\quad5\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The directions are never parallel. The lines intersect precisely when the connector has zero component along their common normal:

\[2 t - 1=0\]
\[t=\frac{1}{2}\]

At this parameter, equate the coordinates of \(\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf u\) and \(\mathbf c+\mu\mathbf v\). The solution is

\[\lambda=3,\qquad\mu=2\]
\[t=\frac{1}{2},\qquad \mathbf h=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\\frac{3}{2}\\1\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\- \frac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}=-2\]

Using the point \(\left(-2,0,-2\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[2 x + 2 y - z=-2\]

(c)

The common normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\- t\end{pmatrix}\), so the distance formula gives

\[\frac{|2 t - 1|}{\sqrt{t^{2} + 2}}=\sqrt{3}\]

Both sides are non-negative and the denominator is strictly positive, so squaring introduces no additional sign condition:

\[\left(t - 5\right) \left(t + 1\right)=0\]

Solving gives

\[t=-1\quad\text{or}\quad5\]

Substitution of each value in the original distance formula gives \(\sqrt{3}\). Both values are admissible.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The common-normal component must be zero; then verify the intersection by solving for the two line parameters.

(b)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(c)

Keep the absolute value until squaring, and check every candidate in the original distance condition.

questions.prompt_html:

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}t - 5\\-3\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-4\\1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

Here \(t\) is a real constant.

Point \(P\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}7\\5\\2\end{pmatrix}\). After using the intersection condition, let \(\Pi\) be the plane containing the two lines.

  1. Find \(t\) so that the lines intersect, and state their intersection point.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact perpendicular distance from \(P\) to \(\Pi\).

    [4]

  3. Find the exact shortest distance from \(P\) to \(l_1\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[t=0,\qquad H=\left(1,-1,4\right)\]

(b)

\[d=2 \sqrt{14}\]

(c)

\[d=\frac{4 \sqrt{1330}}{19}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The two directions have common normal \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\). For an intersection,

\[(\mathbf b-\mathbf a(t))\cdot\mathbf n=- t=0\]

Thus \(t=0\). At this value, \(\lambda=2,\mu=-3\) gives the common point \(\left(1,-1,4\right)\).

(b)

The plane has normal \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and contains \(\left(1,-1,4\right)\), hence its equation is \(x + 3 y - 2 z=-10\).

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|28|}{\sqrt{14}}=2 \sqrt{14}\]

The absolute value ensures a non-negative distance.

(c)

Project \(\mathbf p-\mathbf a\) onto the line direction. The foot has parameter

\[\tau=\frac{(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}=\frac{56}{19}\]
\[\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\tau\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{73}{19}\\- \frac{1}{19}\\\frac{130}{19}\end{pmatrix}\]

Therefore the perpendicular distance is

\[|\mathbf p-\mathbf h|=\frac{4 \sqrt{1330}}{19}\]

Equivalently, use \(|(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf u|/|\mathbf u|\).

questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

The plane \(\Pi\) has equation \(11 x + 10 y - 9 z=7\). Let \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=OC\).

  1. Find the exact perpendicular distance from \(O\) to \(\Pi\).

    [3]

  2. Find the acute angle between \(OAB\) and \(\Pi\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [4]

  3. The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors. Hence give a vector equation of the common perpendicular.

    [7]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[d=\frac{7 \sqrt{302}}{302}\]

(b)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{17 \sqrt{302}}{302}\right)=12.0^\circ\]

(c)

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\10\\-9\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|-7|}{\sqrt{302}}=\frac{7 \sqrt{302}}{302}\]

The absolute value ensures a non-negative distance.

(b)

A normal to \(OAB\) is \(\overrightarrow{OA}\times\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-8\\-12\\9\end{pmatrix}\).

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}8\\12\\-9\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}11\\10\\-9\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|289|}{17 \sqrt{302}}=\frac{17 \sqrt{302}}{302}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{17 \sqrt{302}}{302}\right)=12.0^\circ\]

(c)

Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- 3 \lambda + \mu + 3\\2 \lambda + 1\\4 - \mu\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 13 \lambda + 3 \mu + 7=0\]
\[- 3 \lambda + 2 \mu - 1=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=1,\qquad\mu=2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

A line through \(P\) parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\) is therefore

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

questions.title: A parallel limit that must be treated separately
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\t - 3\\5\end{pmatrix}\]

Here \(t\) is real. Let \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=CD\).

For part (d), take \(t=2\).

  1. Find the value of \(t\) for which the lines are parallel, and show that they are not coincident.

    [2]

  2. For all other values of \(t\), find the shortest distance between the lines.

    [3]

  3. When \(t=4\), find the shortest distance between the two parallel lines. Explain why the previous answer cannot simply be substituted.

    [3]

  4. Find the acute angle between \(ABC\) and \(ABD\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[t=4\]

(b)

\[d=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\]

(c)

\[d=\frac{\sqrt{14}}{2}\]

(d)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{11 \sqrt{1113}}{371}\right)=8.4^\circ\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{CD}=\begin{pmatrix}4 - t\\0\\t - 4\end{pmatrix}\]

This vanishes precisely when \(t=4\). The anchors are not on the same line, so this case gives distinct parallel lines.

The anchor displacement is \(\overrightarrow{AC}=(1,0,2)^T\), which is not a scalar multiple of \((1,2,1)^T\). Thus the parallel lines are distinct.

(b)

For \(t\ne4\), the common normal is parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). The shortest distance is

\[\frac{|t - 4|}{\sqrt{2 \left(t - 4\right)^{2}}}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\]

The cancelled factor is non-zero under the stated restriction.

(c)

Project \(\mathbf p-\mathbf a\) onto the line direction. The foot has parameter

\[\tau=\frac{(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}=\frac{1}{2}\]
\[\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\tau\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{5}{2}\\-2\\\frac{3}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]

Therefore the perpendicular distance is

\[|\mathbf p-\mathbf h|=\frac{\sqrt{14}}{2}\]

Equivalently, use \(|(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf u|/|\mathbf u|\).

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-1\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|33|}{\sqrt{1113}}=\frac{11 \sqrt{1113}}{371}\]

questions.title: A moving line and an exact distance condition
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\t - 2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

Here \(t\) is real. Let \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=CD\).

For parts (b) and (c), use \(t=\frac{1}{11}\).

  1. Find all real values of \(t\) for which the shortest distance is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

    [5]

  2. Find the exact shortest distance from \(D\) to \(AC\).

    [4]

  3. Find the acute angle between \(ABC\) and \(ABD\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[t=\frac{1}{11}\quad\text{or}\quad1\]

(b)

\[d=\frac{3 \sqrt{1005}}{55}\]

(c)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{3 \sqrt{38}}{19}\right)=13.3^\circ\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The common normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\- t\end{pmatrix}\), so the distance formula gives

\[\frac{|2 t - 1|}{\sqrt{t^{2} + 2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\]

Both sides are non-negative and the denominator is strictly positive, so squaring introduces no additional sign condition:

\[\frac{\left(t - 1\right) \left(11 t - 1\right)}{3}=0\]

Solving gives

\[t=\frac{1}{11}\quad\text{or}\quad1\]

Substitution of each value in the original distance formula gives \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Both values are admissible.

(b)

Project \(\mathbf p-\mathbf a\) onto the line direction. The foot has parameter

\[\tau=\frac{(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}=\frac{4}{5}\]
\[\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\tau\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{11}{5}\\-3\\\frac{7}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]

Therefore the perpendicular distance is

\[|\mathbf p-\mathbf h|=\frac{3 \sqrt{1005}}{55}\]

Equivalently, use \(|(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf u|/|\mathbf u|\).

(c)

For plane \(ABC\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\-2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

For plane \(ABD\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}-2\\\frac{12}{11}\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\\frac{10}{11}\end{pmatrix}\]

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}11\\11\\-10\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|54|}{9 \sqrt{38}}=\frac{3 \sqrt{38}}{19}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{3 \sqrt{38}}{19}\right)=13.3^\circ\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Keep the absolute value until squaring, and check every candidate in the original distance condition.

(b)

Find the foot by a scalar product, or use the magnitude of a vector product divided by the direction length.

(c)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

Use the following normals to the two planes:

questions.title: Parallel planes, a section point and a normal line
questions.prompt_html:
The plane \(\Pi_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-4\\2\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

The parameters \(s\) and \(t\) are real.

Point \(A\) is the given plane anchor. Point \(L\) satisfies \(\overrightarrow{OL}=4\overrightarrow{OA}\). Plane \(\Pi_2\) passes through \(L\) and is parallel to \(\Pi_1\). Point \(M\) lies on segment \(AL\) and satisfies \(\overrightarrow{AM}=2\overrightarrow{ML}\).

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi_2\).

    [3]

  2. Find the position vector of \(N\), the foot of the perpendicular from \(O\) to the plane.

    [4]

  3. Find the position vector of \(M\).

    [3]

  4. Find the exact shortest distance from \(M\) to \(ON\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[4 x + 2 y + 5 z=-24\]

(b)

\[\overrightarrow{ON}=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{32}{15}\\- \frac{16}{15}\\- \frac{8}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\overrightarrow{OM}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-12\\6\end{pmatrix}\]

(d)

\[d=\frac{6 \sqrt{145}}{5}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-8\\-4\\-10\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\\5\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\\5\end{pmatrix}=-24\]

Using the point \(\left(-8,-16,8\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[4 x + 2 y + 5 z=-24\]

(b)

The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\\5\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

\[0-45\tau=-24\]
\[\tau=\frac{8}{15}\]

Therefore

\[\overrightarrow{ON}=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{32}{15}\\- \frac{16}{15}\\- \frac{8}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

The vector relation gives \(\mathbf m-\mathbf a=2(\mathbf l-\mathbf m)\), so

\[3\mathbf m=\mathbf a+2\mathbf l=9\mathbf a\]
\[\overrightarrow{OM}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-12\\6\end{pmatrix}\]

(d)

Project \(\mathbf p-\mathbf a\) onto the line direction. The foot has parameter

\[\tau=\frac{(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}=- \frac{2}{5}\]
\[\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\tau\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{8}{5}\\- \frac{4}{5}\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

Therefore the perpendicular distance is

\[|\mathbf p-\mathbf h|=\frac{6 \sqrt{145}}{5}\]

Equivalently, use \(|(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf u|/|\mathbf u|\).

questions.title: Two skew lines and the dihedral angle
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\6\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\5\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\7\\-8\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\4\\-11\end{pmatrix}\]

\[d=2 \sqrt{22}\]

(a)

A common perpendicular direction is

\[\mathbf n=\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

\[d=\frac{|(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|44|}{\sqrt{22}}=2 \sqrt{22}\]

The vector product is non-zero and the scalar product is non-zero, so the lines are non-parallel and non-coplanar: they are skew.

Any non-zero scalar multiple is an equally valid normal.

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}5\\5\\4\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-5\\7\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|33|}{22 \sqrt{15}}=\frac{\sqrt{15}}{10}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{15}}{10}\right)=67.2^\circ\]

questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\6\end{pmatrix}\]

Point \(N\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(O\) to plane \(ABC\). Point \(P\) lies on \(ON\) with \(OP=\frac23ON\). The line \(AP\) meets plane \(OBC\) at \(Q\).

  1. Find a normal to plane \(ABC\) and the exact length \(ON\).

    [4]

  2. Find the position vector of \(Q\).

    [6]

questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad ON=\frac{3 \sqrt{14}}{7}\]

(a)

The side vectors are \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\3\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\\6\end{pmatrix}\). Their cross product is \(\begin{pmatrix}18\\12\\6\end{pmatrix}\), so use normal \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\). The plane equation is \(3 x + 2 y + z=6\). Hence

\[ON=\frac{|6|}{\sqrt{14}}=\frac{3 \sqrt{14}}{7}\]

The perpendicular from the origin is along the normal. Thus

Plane \(OBC\) is \(x=0\). Equating the first component to zero gives \(\lambda=\frac{7}{4}\). Substituting yields

\[\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\\frac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

For plane \(ABQ\), take the vector product of two directions in it:

\[\begin{pmatrix}-2\\3\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\\frac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\\1\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

questions.title: Projecting a whole line onto a plane
questions.prompt_html:
The plane \(\Pi\) has equation

\[3 x + y + z=-11\]

Line \(l\) passes through \(P=\left(2,-1,6\right)\) and has equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\6\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

The orthogonal projection of \(l\) onto \(\Pi\) is the locus of the perpendicular feet of all points of \(l\).

  1. Find \(X\), the point where \(l\) meets \(\Pi\).

    [3]

  2. State a normal \(\mathbf n\) to the plane and calculate \(\mathbf n\times\mathbf w\), where \(\mathbf w\) is the line direction.

    [2]

  3. Find a vector equation of the orthogonal projection of \(l\) onto \(\Pi\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-1\\8\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf n\times\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\7\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-3\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Substitute the line into the plane equation:

\[11+(11)\lambda=-11\]
\[\lambda=-2\]

Since \(11\)\(\ne0\), there is exactly one intersection. Substitution into the line gives

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-1\\8\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Read the normal from the plane equation and evaluate the component vector product:

\[\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\7\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Project a general point \(\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w\) onto the plane. Removing the normal component gives

\[\mathbf h(\lambda)=\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w-\frac{\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w)-d}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n\]

Collect constant and parameter terms:

\[\mathbf h(\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-3\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

The new direction is non-zero and has zero dot product with \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Thus this is a line in the plane, not a single point. Equivalently, a direction is \((\mathbf n\times\mathbf w)\times\mathbf n\).

questions.title: A tetrahedron built from the closest pair
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-6\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}8\\-3\\-5\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

Let \(A\) and \(B\) be the given anchors on \(l_1\) and \(l_2\). The common perpendicular meets them at \(P\) and \(Q\), respectively.

  1. The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors.

    [6]

  2. Find the exact area of triangle \(APQ\).

    [4]

  3. Find the exact volume of tetrahedron \(APQB\). You may use \(V=\frac13\times\text{base area}\times\text{perpendicular height}\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-4\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\operatorname{Area}(APQ)=\frac{3 \sqrt{30}}{2}\]

(c)

\[V=18\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}\mu + 9\\- 2 \lambda + \mu + 3\\- \lambda - 3 \mu - 3\end{pmatrix}\]

questions.title: A normal plane through a perpendicular foot
questions.prompt_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-3\\-5\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\-3\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

Plane \(\Pi\) passes through the first foot \(P\) and is perpendicular to \(l_1\).

A second plane \(\Sigma\) is \(z=0\).

  1. The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors. Hence give a vector equation of the common perpendicular.

    [7]

  2. Give a vector equation of \(\Pi\) in two-parameter form.

    [3]

  3. Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of \(\Pi\) and \(\Sigma\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\3\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}-5\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{7}{2}\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- 2 \lambda + \mu + 6\\6 - \lambda\\- 2 \left(\lambda - 1\right)\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 9 \lambda + 2 \mu + 22=0\]
\[- 2 \lambda + \mu + 6=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=2,\qquad\mu=-2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\3\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

A line through \(P\) parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) is therefore

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Use the known point \(\left(-2,-1,-1\right)\). The independent directions \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}-5\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}\) are parallel to the plane; their cross product is non-zero. Therefore

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}-5\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

A direction of the intersection is perpendicular to both normals:

\[\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence we may take direction \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\). Solving the two plane equations with a convenient coordinate set to zero gives the point \(\left(- \frac{7}{2},0,0\right)\). It satisfies both equations:

\[-7=-7,\qquad 0=0\]

The required line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{7}{2}\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

questions.title: A moving line and an exact distance condition
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\4\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\5\\t - 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Here \(t\) is real. Let \(l_1=AB\) and \(l_2=CD\).

  1. Find all real values of \(t\) for which the shortest distance is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

    [6]

  2. Let \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\) be the planes \(ABD\) for \(t=\frac{3}{13}\) and \(t=1\), respectively. Find their Cartesian equations.

    [4]

  3. Find the acute angle between \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[t=\frac{3}{13}\quad\text{or}\quad1\]

(b)

\[\Pi_1: 75 x + 52 y - 52 z=0\]
\[\Pi_2: 5 x + 4 y - 4 z=0\]

(c)

\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{791 \sqrt{628881}}{628881}\right)=4.1^\circ\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The common normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}t - 2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\), so the distance formula gives

\[\frac{|2 - 3 t|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 4 t + 6}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\]

Both sides are non-negative and the denominator is strictly positive, so squaring introduces no additional sign condition:

\[\frac{2 \left(t - 1\right) \left(13 t - 3\right)}{3}=0\]

Solving gives

\[t=\frac{3}{13}\quad\text{or}\quad1\]

Substitution of each value in the original distance formula gives \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Both values are admissible.

(b)

For \(t=\frac{3}{13}\), \(D=\left(-4,5,- \frac{10}{13}\right)\). A normal to \(ABD\) is

\[\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AD}=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{75}{13}\\-4\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}75\\52\\-52\end{pmatrix}\) and point \(\left(0,0,0\right)\).

\[75 x + 52 y - 52 z=0\]

For \(t=1\), \(D=\left(-4,5,0\right)\). A normal to \(ABD\) is

\[\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AD}=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-4\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\4\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) and point \(\left(0,0,0\right)\).

\[5 x + 4 y - 4 z=0\]

(c)

Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}75\\52\\-52\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}5\\4\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|791|}{\sqrt{628881}}=\frac{791 \sqrt{628881}}{628881}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{791 \sqrt{628881}}{628881}\right)=4.1^\circ\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Keep the absolute value until squaring, and check every candidate in the original distance condition.

(b)

For each admissible value, use AB and AD as the two plane directions.

(c)

Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

(a)

\[d=2 \sqrt{11}\]

(b)

(a)

A common perpendicular direction is

\[\mathbf n=\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]

\[d=\frac{|(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|22|}{\sqrt{11}}=2 \sqrt{11}\]

The vector product is non-zero and the scalar product is non-zero, so the lines are non-parallel and non-coplanar: they are skew.

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}=13\]

Using the point \(\left(4,3,-4\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[3 x + 3 y + 2 z=13\]

(c)

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|-22|}{\sqrt{22}}=\sqrt{22}\]

questions.title: A rotating direction and a common perpendicular
questions.prompt_html:
For \(0\leq t<2\pi\), the lines are

\[l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)}\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

The shortest joining segment is \(PQ\), with \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\).

  1. Find the shortest distance between \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) as a function of \(t\).

    [4]

  2. Find all \(t\) for which the two lines intersect.

    [3]

  3. When \(t=\pi/3\), find the perpendicular distance from \(A\) to plane \(BPQ\), where \(A\) and \(B\) are the line anchors. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[d(t)=\frac{|2 \left(2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 1\right)|}{\sqrt{16 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 5}}\]

(b)

\[t=\frac\pi6,\quad\frac{5\pi}6\]

(c)

\[d=\frac{4 \sqrt{221} \left(-1 + \sqrt{3}\right)}{221}\]
\[d\approx 0.197\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The line directions have vector product

\[\mathbf n(t)=\begin{pmatrix}- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)}\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

This vector never vanishes. The anchor connector has scalar product \(2 \left(2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 1\right)\) with it, so the perpendicular separation is

\[d(t)=\frac{|2 \left(2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 1\right)|}{\sqrt{16 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 5}}\]

A zero numerator corresponds to intersecting, not skew, lines; the same expression then gives distance zero.

(b)

The cross product never vanishes because its second component is -1. Thus zero distance means intersection. The numerator is zero when

\[2 \left(2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 1\right)=0\]
\[\sin t=\frac12\]

In the stated interval this gives

\[t=\frac\pi6,\quad\frac{5\pi}6\]

(c)

The plane contains the direction \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\- 2 \sqrt{3}\\0\end{pmatrix}\) of \(l_2\) and the common normal \(\begin{pmatrix}- 2 \sqrt{3}\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\). Hence a plane normal is

\[\begin{pmatrix}4 \sqrt{3}\\2\\-13\end{pmatrix}\]

The normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}4 \sqrt{3}\\2\\-13\end{pmatrix}\). The perpendicular distance is the absolute normal component:

\[d=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d_0|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|4 \left(-1 + \sqrt{3}\right)|}{\sqrt{221}}=\frac{4 \sqrt{221} \left(-1 + \sqrt{3}\right)}{221}\]

The absolute value ensures a non-negative distance.

\[d\approx 0.197\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the vector product of the directions and project the anchor connector onto it.

(b)

Set the distance numerator to zero and solve over the full specified angular interval.

(c)

Divide the absolute residual in the plane equation by the length of its normal.

questions.title: Two possible sides of a plane
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\4\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}t + 4\\t + 3\\t + 2\end{pmatrix}\]

The parameter \(t\) is real.

  1. Find a Cartesian equation of \(ABC\).

    [2]

  2. Find all values of \(t\) for which the perpendicular distance from \(P\) to plane \(ABC\) is \(2 \sqrt{3}\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[x + y + z=9\]

(b)

\[t=-2\quad\text{or}\quad t=2\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}=9\]

Using the point \(\left(3,4,2\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[x + y + z=9\]

(b)

The perpendicular distance from P to ABC is

\[\frac{|3 t|}{\sqrt{3}}=|t|\sqrt{3}\]

Equate this to \(2 \sqrt{3}\); since the normal is non-zero,

\[|t|=2\]
\[t=-2\quad\text{or}\quad t=2\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

(b)

The absolute value gives two possible sides of the plane.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form two directions and their vector product.
Obtain a non-zero normal \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Substitute a known point to obtain the constant. Obtain \(x + y + z=9\).

questions.title: The vector product as area and height
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\4\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

  1. Calculate \(\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact area of triangle \(ABC\).

    [2]

  3. Find the exact shortest distance from \(C\) to \(AB\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\\7\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\operatorname{Area}(ABC)=\frac{\sqrt{59}}{2}\]

(c)

\[d=\frac{\sqrt{826}}{14}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Use \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\).

\[\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\\7\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

The two side vectors from \(A\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Their vector product is

\[\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\\7\end{pmatrix}\]

Its magnitude is the area of the parallelogram, so the triangle has half this area:

\[\operatorname{Area}(ABC)=\frac{\sqrt{59}}{2}\]

(c)

Project \(\mathbf p-\mathbf a\) onto the line direction. The foot has parameter

\[\tau=\frac{(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}=\frac{5}{14}\]
\[\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\tau\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{13}{14}\\\frac{16}{7}\\\frac{33}{14}\end{pmatrix}\]

Therefore the perpendicular distance is

\[|\mathbf p-\mathbf h|=\frac{\sqrt{826}}{14}\]

Equivalently, use \(|(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf u|/|\mathbf u|\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use displacements from the same vertex.

(b)

Use half the magnitude of the vector product of two sides from the same vertex.

(c)

Find the foot by a scalar product, or use the magnitude of a vector product divided by the direction length.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the correct vector product. Take half its magnitude to obtain \(\frac{\sqrt{59}}{2}\).
Obtain the foot \(\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{13}{14}\\\frac{16}{7}\\\frac{33}{14}\end{pmatrix}\) or the correct vector product. Obtain distance \(\frac{\sqrt{826}}{14}\).

questions.title: A compact tetrahedron calculation
questions.prompt_html:
Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

The volume of a tetrahedron is \(\frac13\times\text{base area}\times\text{perpendicular height}\).

  1. Find \(\overrightarrow{OA}\times\overrightarrow{OB}\).

    [1]

  2. Deduce the exact area of triangle \(OAB\).

    [1]

  3. Find the exact volume of tetrahedron \(OABC\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\\-6\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\text{Area}=\frac{9}{2}\]

(c)

\[V=2\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\\-6\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\text{Area}=\tfrac12|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|=\tfrac12\sqrt{81}=\frac{9}{2}\]

(c)

Plane OAB has normal \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\\-6\end{pmatrix}\). Its distance from C is

\[h=12/9=\frac{4}{3}\]
\[V=\tfrac13\times\frac{9}{2}\times\frac{4}{3}=2\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Calculate the three components of the vector product.

(b)

The vector product gives twice the triangle area.

(c)

Use OAB as the base and the normal component of OC as the height.
